ranges.en: Mishna: a donkey whose offspring or ownership is shared with or transferred to a gentile is exempt from firstborn status.
Why are all these mishna examples needed if the basic principle is already clear?
Each case is taught separately: buying the fetus suggests sanctity, while selling it would invite penalty, so the exemption must be stated.
Why is the partnership case needed as a separate example?
It excludes Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a partnership animal with a gentile is firstborn-obligated.
Why does the mishna also need to state the case of one who receives a donkey from a gentile?
Why repeat the case of giving a donkey to a gentile in receivership, since it seems already covered?
It is taught so the owner is not penalized, lest the case be confused with one where the gentile has no rights to the offspring.
A mishna elsewhere permits selling a damaged animal or a riding horse to a gentile, according to Rabbi Yehuda and ben Beteira.
A dilemma: does Rabbi Yehuda's damaged-animal rationale apply to a fetus, which is its natural state rather than a defect?
A mishna is brought: selling a fetus is forbidden, and the mishna records no dissent from Rabbi Yehuda.
Objection: if silence proves agreement in the other cases, Rabbi Yehuda would also agree here, which contradicts the earlier view.
Rather, he does disagree, but the mishna simply does not teach his opinion in these cases.
A baraita shows Rabbi Yehuda disagreeing: the receiver gives half the value to a priest, and the giver is penalized by buying out the gentile's share.

ranges.en: Asks whether the baraita's prohibition refers to the fetus rather than to the animal itself.
No, the prohibition concerns the mother animal, which is why the gentile sale is penalized.
Objects that the masculine wording of the baraita suggests the penalty concerns the fetus.
Corrects the wording to the feminine form, which refers to the mother animal.
Objects that the priest receiving the whole value makes sense only if the fetus is meant.
Speaks of a pregnant animal fattened on shares; since the mother is penalized, the fetus is penalized too.
Rav Ashi offers his suggested resolution.
Baraita: a damaged animal may be sold only if it cannot be healed, implying a fetus, which can later work, is prohibited.
Introduces the mishna on selling a donkey's fetus to a gentile, which is exempt from firstborn status.
Suggests the mishna rejects Rabbi Yehuda's view, which permits selling a damaged animal, and a fetus is likewise unable to work.
Replies that Rabbi Yehuda's leniency is consistent: a fetus is in its natural state, so it is not damaged.
Brings a baraita on receiving and giving animals to gentiles, with Rabbi Yehuda's split and the Sages' penalty for the giver.
Asks again whether the prohibition refers to the fetus rather than the animal.
No, it is the animal itself that may not be sold, so the penalty applies to the mother.
Repeats the objection that the masculine wording indicates the fetus.
Teach the feminine wording, which refers to the mother animal.
Objects that the priest receiving the whole value makes sense only if the fetus is meant.
Pregnant animal fattened on shares; the penalty for the mother extends to the fetus.
Rav Ashi again offers his resolution.
Baraita: a damaged animal may be sold only if incurable, so a fetus, which will later work, is prohibited.
Raises the dilemma: is selling an animal only for its fetuses permitted, according to Rabbi Yehuda and according to the Rabbis?
On Rabbi Yehuda's view: perhaps only damaged animals are permitted, or all such sales are permitted since the animal is separated in the sale.
The same alternatives on the Rabbis' view: they might prohibit only damaged animals, or prohibit fetus-only sales of unblemished animals too.
Objects: if the Rabbis' reason is confusion, a baraita shows they cite breeding and fetuses, so they should prohibit fetus sales too.
Explains the Rabbis' real point: confusion is their reason, while Rabbi Yehuda treats a damaged animal like one sold for slaughter.
Objects that the slaughter analogy fails, since a damaged animal is bred and gives birth, delaying its slaughter.
Replies that he will address this only if the animal gives birth, since such an animal does not accept a male.
Brings a mishna on receivership: it omits the phrase that the arrangement is not permitted, suggesting it is allowed.
Objects: by the same reasoning, the partnership case omits that phrase too, so partnership would also seem permitted.
Cites Shmuel's father, who prohibited partnership with a gentile, deriving this from a verse forbidding mention of idolatry.
Rather, the tanna taught only the sale case, and the same rule covers partnership and receivership.
Asks why the tanna specifically cites the case of sale.
Because sale is the primary transaction, so it is the one the tanna names.
Repeats the baraita on receiving and giving animals to gentiles, with Rabbi Yehuda's split and the Sages' penalty.
The Sages hold that while a gentile owns part of the animal, its offspring is exempt from firstborn status.

ranges.en: Asks whether the baraita's prohibition on receivership refers to the animal itself rather than its fetus.
No, it refers to an existing fetus in a pregnant animal, so only sale of a non-pregnant animal's fetus rights is allowed.
The masculine wording of the baraita is precise, referring to the fetus, and it supports Reish Lakish's view.
Reish Lakish holds that one who sells large livestock to a gentile is penalized to repurchase it for up to ten times its value.
Asks whether the phrase up to ten times its value is meant exactly or only as an approximate figure.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling on selling a slave to a gentile, with a penalty of up to one hundred times its value, is brought as a proof.
A slave is different, since each day of work for the gentile removes the master's obligation to perform mitzvot.
Another version has Reish Lakish saying the penalty for selling large livestock is up to one hundred times its value.
A baraita on giving an animal in receivership sets the penalty at ten times its value, which contradicts Reish Lakish's one hundred.
The two cases differ: a sale fully separates the animal from the Jew, while receivership leaves it partly his, so the penalty is lighter.
Asks whether the one hundred times figure of Reish Lakish is meant exactly or only approximately.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's slave ruling, with a penalty of up to ten times the value, is brought to show the figure is not exact.
A slave is different, since the slave does not return to the owner, so the Sages penalized the owner in another way.
If the animal is penalized more because it returns to its owner, the penalty should exceed the slave's by only one additional amount.
Selling a slave is an uncommon matter, and the Sages did not issue decrees concerning uncommon matters.
The Rabbis hold that as long as a gentile's hand is involved, the offspring is exempt from firstborn status.
Rabbi Yehoshua says that both sides interpreted the same verse in accordance with their own views.
Cites the verse Exodus 13:2 about every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel.
The Rabbis read the verse as requiring that the entire firstborn be owned by a Jew for it to have firstborn status.
Rabbi Yehuda reads the same verse as applying whenever any portion of the firstborn is owned by a Jew.
Alternatively, all agree the verse requires a Jewish majority; each side reads the word all as filling or diminishing that requirement.
Asks how large a gentile's partnership must be for the animal to be exempt from firstborn status according to the Rabbis.
Rav Huna says that even if the gentile owns only the animal's ear, the animal is exempt.
Rav Naḥman objects: the priest could tell the gentile to take his ear and leave, so the animal would be firstborn.
Rav Ḥisda holds that a gentile partner in a limb whose removal kills the animal exempts it; Rava holds that a tereifa-causing limb does.
Asks what principle the amoraim disagree about.
They disagree about whether a tereifa can live long; one holds it cannot, so the gentile owns an essential part, the other that it can live.
The Sages told Rav Pappa that the rulings do not conflict: Rav Huna's applies to the fetus, while the others' applies to the mother.
Rav Pappa rejects the distinction: the verse all the firstborn and the verse on all livestock demand full Jewish ownership for both fetus and mother, so the rules should match.
Cites the verses on firstborn that emerges from an animal and on firstborn from animals, to show that a fetus is also sacred.
Non-viable newborns have no non-sacred element mixed in, so the all-firstborn rule applies, but a gentile's share in fetuses makes it inapplicable.
Narrates that Rabbi Elazar missed the study hall and found Rabbi Asi there.
Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Asi what the Sages said in the study hall.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that even a slight blemish caused by removing the gentile's share disqualifies the animal from firstborn status.
Cites the mishna: a ewe that bore a goat-like offspring, or a goat that bore a ewe-like one, is exempt from firstborn status.
If the offspring has some of the marks of its species, it is obligated, but Rabbi Yoḥanan says it is a permanent blemish, so it may be slaughtered outside the Temple.
Asks why Rabbi Yoḥanan's first ruling is needed, and what his point about a permanent blemish adds beyond it.
Answers that the point is already taught: a lamb whose mouth resembles a pig's has a blemish, so an altered appearance is a blemish.
Objects that the pig-mouth case differs, since there the change is into a species without firstborn sanctity, while here it stays within the sanctified species.
Notes that the mishna also teaches the case of one eye large and one small as a blemish.
A tanna explains that a large eye is as large as a calf's and a small eye is as small as a goose's.
Asks whether the large-eye blemish really stems from the change in appearance, which would make Rabbi Yoḥanan's statement a novelty.
No, the large eye is a blemish because the animal has an overly large limb, a blemish listed in the Torah, which is reasonable.
Mishna: these blemishes, whether permanent or transient, disqualify priests too, and further, both eyes being large or small disqualifies a man.
Cites the verse that any man of Aaron's seed is required, so a priest must have the ordinary appearance of Aaron's line.
For animals, both eyes large or both small is not a blemish, while one large and one small is.
Asks whether the blemish of one large and one small eye comes from change, since both large or both small should then also be blemished.
Deviation from the normal look is a blemish; both eyes large or small is not a deviation, because it reflects extreme health or extreme weakness.
Recounts that a female convert whose gentile brothers fattened her animals asked Rava whether firstborn status applies to their offspring.
Rava replies that no one heeds Rabbi Yehuda's view that an animal partly owned by a gentile is obligated as firstborn.
Narrates that Rav Mari bar Raḥel transferred the ears of firstborn fetuses to a gentile, yet still treated the animals as firstborn in shearing and labor, and that his animals died.
Asks why he transferred their ears to a gentile if he prohibited shearing and labor and gave them to priests.
He acted to avoid the priests coming to a mishap with them, improperly shearing or working them.
Asks what the reason was that Rav Mari's animals died, if he acted to avoid mishap.
They died because he abrogated their sanctity by selling their ears.
Objects that Rav Yehuda permits blemishing a firstborn fetus, so Rav Mari's sale should similarly be permitted, and the answer distinguishes the sanctity of altar and priest.
Alternatively, Rav Mari knew how to make a complete transfer, but others copied him without a complete transfer and suffered a mishap.
Mishna: priests and Levites are exempt from redeeming a firstborn donkey.
A fortiori argument: if the Levites exempted Israel's firstborn donkeys in the wilderness, they surely exempt their own donkeys.

ranges.en: Asks whether the priests and Levites actually exempted the Israelite firstborn children and donkeys, given the mishna's wording.
Cites the verse in Numbers about taking the Levites in exchange for the firstborn, and the Levites' animals in exchange for their animals.
Abaye explains the mishna as teaching that priests' and Levites' own firstborn animals are exempt, by an a fortiori argument from the wilderness.
Rava objects that the mishna says they exempted the Israelite firstborn, not their own animals, and that the exemption from kosher firstborns would then follow too.
Rava reinterprets the mishna: the priests and Levites exempted themselves, by an a fortiori argument from the Levites' sanctity in the wilderness.
Asks from where we know that the Levites' non-kosher animals are also not counted as firstborn.
The verse on redeeming the firstborn of man and of non-kosher animals is juxtaposed, so the rules match, and the animals need not be redeemed.
Rav Safra objects to Abaye: if the Levite's animals are exempt only when a lamb abrogates the Israelite sanctity, the rule should depend on that lamb.
Rav Safra asks: why should only a Levite firstborn over one month old have his status abrogated, since only that age abrogates Israelite sanctity.
Asks why a Levite mother's firstborn son is exempt from the five-sela redemption, since women were not included in the exchange.
Not difficult: the Torah ties firstborn status to the womb, so the mother's Levite status exempts the child.
Rav Safra challenges again: Aaron was not in the Levite count, so his own firstborn status should not be abrogated, as the baraita on the dots over his name shows.
The verse says all the Levites, which juxtaposes them, so even a Levite who did not himself abrogate Israelite sanctity is abrogated.
Asks from where we derive that priests, including Aaron, are subject to the same rule as the Levites.
Cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: in twenty-four places priests are called Levites, as in the Ezekiel verse about the priests the Levites, sons of Zadok.

ranges.en: Asks from where we know that the Levites' exemption from firstborn status applies for all generations.
Cites the verse in Numbers that the Levites shall be Mine, read as them remaining in their present state of sanctity.
Asks how we know that the redemption animal is specifically a lamb.
Rav Ḥisda: the verses use silver and lamb for later generations, so these are the redemption items for both periods.
Analogy: just as silver was used in both periods, so the lamb is used for redemption in both periods.
Objects that silver is special because it also redeems consecrated property and second tithe, which lambs do not.
Instead, the verse on redeeming the firstborn of man and non-kosher animals is juxtaposed, so the redemption method is the same in both periods.
Rabbi Ḥanina holds that one lamb of a Levite exempted several firstborn donkeys of Israelites.
Abaye: the verse counts the surplus of firstborn humans but not of animals, showing that one animal sufficed for many donkeys.
Asks whether the Israelites simply had few animals, so their donkeys did not outnumber the Levite lambs.
Do not think so: the verse on the great livestock of Reuben and Gad shows the Israelites owned many animals.
Perhaps the Levites' ordinary non-firstborn animals matched the number of Israelite firstborn animals, so no surplus arises.
The verse uses the singular behemat for the Levites' animal and the plural for the Israelites', showing one animal was exchanged for many.
Asks whether behemat might refer to many animals, as in the Jonah verse with many animals.
If so, the verse would have written the word in a different form; the phrasing teaches that one Levite lamb exempted many donkeys.
Rava: a mishna also supports this, saying the owner may redeem many donkeys with the same lamb, and Rabbi Ḥanina is explaining it.
The reason the same lamb may redeem many donkeys is that one Levite lamb exempts several Israelite firstborn donkeys.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that firstborn animals and sons born in the wilderness were sanctified, based on the command to sanctify all firstborn, while Reish Lakish disagrees.
Reish Lakish derives from the verses about entering the land and then setting apart the firstborn that wilderness-born firstborn were not sanctified.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects from a mishna that before the Tabernacle was set up, firstborn performed service, implying wilderness-born firstborn were sanctified.
Reish Lakish replies that the mishna refers to firstborn who left Egypt, since an infant in its first year cannot perform service.
Asks why the objector raised the point at all, since it is obvious that Egypt-born firstborn served in the Tabernacle's early years.
Explains the difficulty: if sanctity lapsed, Egypt-born firstborn would also have lost sanctity, and Reish Lakish says no proof follows from this.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects from a baraita that on the day the Tabernacle was set up, firstborn animal offerings were brought, implying wilderness-born firstborn were sanctified.
Reish Lakish replies that this refers to the firstborn who left Egypt, already sanctified there.
The baraita itself implies that the firstborn were offered only from that day onward, which supports Reish Lakish.
Reish Lakish objects that the baraita implies firstborn animals were offered only on that day and not thereafter, so the wilderness-born were not sanctified.
The baraita means that from that day onward all those offerings were brought, not just on that day.
Asks what the baraita then teaches us.
It teaches that from that day the offerings were brought, while before the Tabernacle they were not, so obligatory offerings were not brought on private altars.
Baraita: the firstborn were sanctified in three places, in Egypt, in the wilderness, and on entering the land, citing a verse for each, implying wilderness sanctity.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the firstborn were commanded to be sanctified in three places, but in some of them they were not actually sanctified.
Rav Pappa objects: the wilderness firstborn were counted from a month old, so they must have been sanctified in the wilderness.
Restates the dispute: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds they were sanctified and not ceased, while Reish Lakish holds they were sanctified only until the counting.

The Gemara asks what the reason is for Rabbi Yochanan's view, given Reish Lakish's scriptural basis.
Rabbi Elazar reports a dream about Rabbi Yochanan, presenting his explanation as a proper matter.
A verse with the phrase 'Mine they shall be' is cited to show the firstborns keep their sanctity.

That verse is needed for the teaching of the school of Rabbi Yishmael about performing this mitzva.
Rav Mordekhai tells Rav Ashi that the two sides of the dispute are taught in the reverse order.
Rabbi Yochanan holds the firstborns were not sanctified in the wilderness, while Reish Lakish holds they were.
Rav Ashi objects that Rav Mordekhai is reversing both the objections and Rabbi Elazar's dream account.
Rav Mordekhai replies that Rabbi Yochanan meant the firstborns needed no consecration, a view Reish Lakish rejected.
The Gemara asks why the alternative version was needed if it amounts to the same dispute as the tradition.
It teaches that a person must repeat a teaching using the precise wording of his own teacher.
Kontrokos asks Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai where the 22,000 firstborn Levites went, given the larger family counts.
Rabban Yochanan replies that the three hundred extra Levites were firstborns, and a firstborn cannot abrogate another's sanctity; Abaye adds his own reasoning.
Kontrokos raises a second difficulty about the silver counts, the sums of the Tabernacle collection and the casting.
Kontrokos asks whether Moses was a thief, a gambler, or unskilled in accounting, since half the silver was not returned.
Rabban Yochanan replies that Moses was a trustworthy, skilled treasurer and the Sanctuary maneh was double the standard value.
Rav Aḥai asks what difficulty prompted Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai to give this answer.
Rav Aḥai proposes that one hundred talents were for the sockets while the rest went to the treasury.
The Gemara answers that another verse gives the total collected as one hundred talents, refuting that proposal.
The Gemara asks from where Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai derived that the Sanctuary maneh was double the standard maneh.
If the proof comes from the verse Kontrokos cited, the weight of the extra silver coins is counted only in small units.
If the maneh were standard, the verse should have stated the sum as 101 talents and eleven maneh instead.
Since the verse counts only in small units, it follows that the Sanctuary maneh was double the standard maneh.
Perhaps the verse counts large sums in talents but small sums in shekels, so the proof does not hold.
The brass offering verse shows the Sanctuary maneh was double, since the extra maneh were counted in small coins.
Perhaps the verse counts large units in talents and small units in shekels, so the proof fails here too.
Rav Ḥisda derives the Sanctuary maneh's double value from the Ezekiel verse on the shekel and maneh weights.

Rabbi Ḥanina reports asking Rabbi Eliezer why firstborn donkeys differ from firstborn horses and camels in redemption.
Rabbi Eliezer says it is a decree of the verse, and also because donkeys helped Israel leave Egypt.
Rabbi Ḥanina asks what the word Rephidim means in the verse about Amalek.
Rabbi Eliezer says Rephidim is a place name, while Rabbi Yehoshua says it alludes to Israel growing lax in the Torah.
Rabbi Ḥanina asks what the word Shittim means in the verse about Israel dwelling there.
Rabbi Eliezer says Shittim is a place name, while Rabbi Yehoshua says it alludes to their engagement in nonsense.
The same tanna'im dispute the verse about calling the people to their gods' offerings, offering different explanations of why.
The Mishna teaches that a cow that bore a donkey-like offspring, or a donkey that bore a horse-like one, is exempt from firstborn status.
The verse about the firstborn donkey, stated twice, requires both the mother and the offspring to be donkeys.
A kosher mother bearing a non-kosher-like offspring may be eaten, but a non-kosher mother bearing a kosher-like offspring may not.
The Gemara cites a mishna on a ewe bearing a goat-like offspring: exempt, but obligated if it has some of the mother's features.
The Gemara asks from where these matters are derived.
Rav Yehuda says the matters are derived from a verse, as he says it is stated in Scripture.
The verse says the firstborn of an ox, lamb or goat must match its mother, so the word firstborn is not superfluous.
One might think an offspring with some of the mother's features is exempt, but the word but teaches otherwise.
The Gemara asks why the tanna cites firstborn twice for the cow, rather than the verse Rav Yehuda interprets.
Rav Yehuda follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, whose baraita derives from each verse that the offspring must fully resemble its mother.
One might think the rule applies even with partial features, but the word but teaches a distinction in this case.
The Gemara asks what the tanna of the mishna and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili disagree about.
The tanna of the mishna holds the Torah revealed the rule for firstborn donkeys and kosher firstborns alike, both with sanctity of value.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds the rule is revealed for inherent sanctity and extends to sanctity of value by a gezera shava.
The Gemara asks why the tanna of the mishna needs the repeated firstborn wording, given the other derivation.
It is needed to teach the burning of the sacrificial fats, following the interpretation of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina asks why fats are mentioned separately for the firstborn ox, lamb, and goat.
Each mention is necessary, since any single animal alone might have been thought to be the only one with the burning obligation.
The Gemara challenges why one of the three cases cannot be derived from the other two.
Each case has a feature the others lack, such as Paschal, communal idolatry, or altar increase, so none can be derived from the rest.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yosei HaGelili reads the verse, if it is needed for burning the fats.
If the verse taught only burning, the repeated firstborn would be superfluous, so it must teach the mother-resemblance rule.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yosei HaGelili does with the repeated firstborn of a donkey phrase.
A baraita says the repetition excludes horses and camels, which would otherwise be included from the verse on non-kosher animals.
The repeated phrase may instead mean only firstborn donkeys are redeemed with a lamb, while horses and camels use other items.

ranges.en: The repeated phrase firstborn of a donkey, said twice, teaches that donkeys alone are obligated, excluding horses and camels.
Rav Aḥai objects that a single mention would have included all non-kosher animals, so the repetition does not prove exclusion.
Rav Aḥai answers that the second mention is needed to exclude horses and camels from the lamb redemption, though they still need redemption.
If only exclusion from lamb redemption were meant, the verse would have written it once; the repetition must teach exclusion of horses and camels.
The Gemara asks how the tanna of our mishna derives the exclusion of horses and camels from the repeated phrase.
Rav Pappa derives it from a generalization and detail in the verse on livestock, limiting the firstborn to the animals specified.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yosei HaGelili responds to this derivation.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds the donkey is not in the generalization, while the Rabbis read the vav as reincorporating it.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yosei HaGelili responds in the other direction.
If the donkey were included, the Torah would not need the vav or repeated word; the Rabbis say the sanctity types require the interposition.
A dilemma is raised: what is the halakha for a cow that bore a donkey-like offspring that has some of the mother's features?
Perhaps the ewe-goat rule extends to kosher species; perhaps the cow-donkey case differs since their sanctity types differ.
If mixed sanctity types do not matter, what is the status of a donkey that bore a horse-like offspring, a non-kosher case?
Similarly, what is the status of a cow that bore a horse-like offspring, where the mother is kosher and the offspring is not?
A baraita states that a kosher mother bearing non-kosher offspring is exempt unless it has some features, which proves the case of the cow and donkey.
The Gemara asks whether the second baraita's last clause refers to both cases.
No, it refers only to a cow that bore a donkey-like offspring.
The Gemara asks why the baraita teaches a donkey bearing a horse-like offspring, and whether that case is necessary to state.
It is needed, because one might think the cow-donkey exemption is due to differing species traits such as horns and hooves.
The mishna teaches that offspring's consumption follows its mother: kosher-mother offspring is permitted, non-kosher-mother offspring prohibited.
The Gemara asks why the mishna needs to state the concluding explanation about kosher and non-kosher offspring.
It is a mnemonic to avoid reversing the rule, so that one follows the mother's status, not the offspring's appearance.
The Gemara asks from where these matters are derived.
A verse excluding the cud-chewing split-hoofed animal born of a non-kosher mother shows the mother's status governs consumption.

ranges.en: A verse says the camel is impure, meaning a non-kosher animal born to a kosher animal is kosher, not impure.
Rabbi Shimon holds the repeated word camel teaches that a camel born from a cow is also non-kosher and forbidden.
The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the repeated word camel, given Rabbi Shimon's reading.
One occurrence forbids the camel itself and the other forbids its milk, while Rabbi Shimon uses it to forbid the milk.
The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Shimon derives that camel's milk is forbidden.
He derives it from the word et in the phrase the camel, while the Rabbis do not expound the particle et.
Shimon HaAmasoni expounded every et in the Torah, but stopped on a verse where et was needed, and his students asked why.
Rabbi Akiva later taught that the et in the fear verse includes Torah scholars, so Rabbis follow the view that et is not expounded.
Rav Aḥa son of Rava challenges Rav Ashi: without the derivation, one would think milk of a non-kosher animal is permitted.
The Gemara asks how this differs from a baraita on creeping animals, whose juices and gravies are forbidden.
Rav Ashi explains the verse was needed because milk's permissibility is itself a novelty, so non-kosher milk might be thought permitted.
If the nursing woman's milk comes from disjointed limbs rather than blood, why does the Torah need a verse to forbid non-kosher milk?
The verse was needed because milk resembles a severed limb, which is generally permitted, so non-kosher milk might be thought permitted too.
The Gemara asks from where we derive that the milk of a kosher animal is permitted.
The prohibition of meat cooked in milk suggests milk alone is permitted, since the verse forbids only the combination.
Milk alone could be forbidden for eating but permitted for benefit, while meat with milk is forbidden for benefit too.
According to Rabbi Shimon, who permits benefit from meat cooked in milk, the verse's mention of both still has a purpose.
Consecrated animals' meat may be eaten but not their milk, so non-sacred kosher milk must be permitted.
The distinction may concern benefit rather than consumption: non-sacred milk is forbidden to eat but permitted to benefit from.
Proverbs says goats' milk suffices for food, so goats' milk must be a kosher food.
Perhaps the verse refers to selling the milk as merchandise rather than eating it.
Samuel says the captain received ten cheeses, showing dairy products were eaten during the war.
Perhaps the cheeses too were meant for sale as merchandise.
It is not normal during war to trade, so the cheese was clearly for eating, proving dairy is permitted.
The land flowing with milk and honey, and the invitation to buy wine and milk, both show milk is permitted to eat.
If the repetition teaches halakhot, do the double words for hare, rock badger, and swine also teach separate halakhot?
The doubled names are needed for a baraita about the shesua and the ra'a, and an extra halakha is derived only where no other reading exists.
A baraita says a ewe bearing a goat-like offspring, and the reverse, are exempt, but Rabbi Shimon requires head and most of body to match.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Shimon requires head and body resemblance also for permissibility of eating.
For firstborn status the verse requires full resemblance, but for eating Rabbi Shimon's camel prohibition may apply only to ordinary-looking camels.

ranges.en: Is the offspring that resembles its mother permitted to eat, or does Rabbi Shimon require head and body resemblance for eating too?
A baraita says a kosher mother's non-kosher offspring is forbidden, but with head and body resemblance it is firstborn, implying eating also requires resemblance.
The resemblance requirement concerns only firstborn status, since the baraita shifts from eating to firstborn; eating needs only partial resemblance.
Rabbi Shimon requires resemblance for eating too; the separate mention for firstborn only teaches that partial resemblance suffices there.
A baraita on the camel verse says offspring with one maternal trait is permitted, provided the impregnation came from a kosher male.
A baraita states Rabbi Yehoshua's view that a lamb is kosher only if both its father and mother are sheep.
Rabbi Eliezer holds the verse adds to what is permitted, permitting offspring even when only the mother is kosher.
The baraita's tanna follows Rabbi Shimon's view that a non-kosher offspring of a kosher animal is non-kosher.
The tanna agrees with Rabbi Shimon on one point and disagrees on the other, so the baraita proves nothing about Rabbi Shimon.
Can a kosher animal become pregnant from a non-kosher animal at all, as the baraita assumes?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says animals of different species or kinds never conceive, except per Rabbi Eliezer, who allows domesticated and wild mixing.
Rabbi Yirmeya says the case is a kosher mother impregnated by a cow-born animal, and the tanna again follows Rabbi Shimon on one point only.
Does Rabbi Eliezer hold that a result caused by both permitted and forbidden elements is permitted, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds it forbidden?
A tereifa's offspring case shows the opposite: Rabbi Eliezer forbids it on the altar, so the view is reversed.
Rabbi Eliezer holds that a result of both forbidden and permitted causes is forbidden, but this case differs because the verse repeats seh.
Rabbi Yehoshua holds a result of both causes is permitted generally, but here the plural lamb wording shows the father must be a lamb too.
A baraita on the camel verse states that if head and body resemble the mother, the offspring is permitted, showing Rabbi Shimon requires it for eating too.
The mishna teaches that what emerges from a non-kosher animal is non-kosher, and what emerges from a kosher animal is kosher.
Rav Sheshet is asked about the status of donkey urine, similar to donkey milk, and whether the same applies to horses and camels.
Horse and camel urine is not turbid like milk, so no dilemma arose for them; donkey urine is turbid, which is why the question concerned it.
Does donkey urine get excreted from the body and forbidden, or is the turbidity merely the heat of the flesh with water passing through?
Rav Sheshet cites the mishna, which says emerges from a non-kosher animal rather than from its body, settling the question about urine.

ranges.en: Any type of non-kosher substance is forbidden, and donkey urine, resembling donkey milk, falls under this prohibition.
Some say the dilemma concerned donkey urine specifically, since horse and camel urine is not drunk by people, unlike donkey urine.
Rav Sheshet answers from the mishna: what emerges from a non-kosher animal is non-kosher, and donkey urine is therefore forbidden.
A baraita permits bee honey because it is not an excretion of the body, so donkey urine, ejected unchanged, should be permitted.
Rav Sheshet follows Rabbi Yaakov, who holds that the Merciful One exempted honey from the rule on non-kosher emissions.
A baraita, per Rabbi Yaakov, derives from the verse that one may eat these winged creatures but not non-kosher winged creatures.
The Gemara asks why this inference is needed, since non-kosher winged creatures are explicitly forbidden, and what the inference then adds.
The baraita includes bee honey as permitted and excludes gizzin and wasp honey, since bee honey alone bears no modifier.
The Gemara asks in accordance with whose opinion the baraita holds gizzin and wasp honey not susceptible to impurity and permitted.
The baraita implies that other honeys need specific intent to become susceptible to impurity, while bee honey does not, since it is normally eaten.
Rav Safra explains that the discharge from a fallow deer's womb is the hart's semen, not eggs, so it is permitted.
Rav Huna holds that the fetal sac born opposite a donkey's face is permitted, since it is merely a secretion and not part of the body.
Rav Ḥisda cites a baraita declaring the skin opposite a newborn's face pure whether alive or dead, supporting Rav Huna's view.
Rav Huna answers that the baraita addresses only mixed life and death cases, so it does not prove the view.
Rav Ḥisda cites a baraita stating the skin is pure whether both are alive or both dead, which refutes Rav Huna's reading.
Rav Huna concedes that if the baraita is taught as stated, he cannot dispute it.
The mishna teaches that a kosher fish swallowed by a non-kosher fish is permitted, while the reverse is forbidden since the host is not its place of development.
The mishna's wording implies the permitted case requires seeing the swallowing, so without seeing it, the fish is forbidden.
A baraita explains the concern: a non-kosher fish spawns live young, while a kosher fish lays eggs, so a found fish may have been spawned.
If so, even seeing the swallowing should not matter, since the swallowed fish may have been digested while the found one was spawned.
Rav Sheshet, Rav Pappa, and Rav Naḥman each locate the found fish in an unusual place, explaining why it was not spawned by the host.
Rav Ashi says the majority of fish spawn their own kind, so a fish found inside is treated as if swallowed in our presence.
The baraita restates that non-kosher fish spawn live young, kosher fish lay eggs, and bats, though they lay eggs, nurse their young.

ranges.en: Dolphins give birth to live young like humans do, according to the opening claim.
The Gemara asks what kind of creatures dolphins are.
Rav Yehuda explains that dolphins are creatures called sons of the sea.
A baraita holds that a male whose testicles are external has offspring born live, while internal testicles mean the female lays eggs.
Shmuel holds wild and domestic geese are different kinds, yet both lay eggs, which contradicts the baraita's testicle rule.
The baraita means external reproductive organs, and the wild goose's organ is internal even though its testicles are external.
A baraita states that a species mating by day gives birth by day, one mating by night gives birth by night, and both gives both.
The baraita's examples: the chicken mates by day, the bat at night, and humans and similar creatures both.
The Gemara asks what halakhic difference it makes whether an animal gives birth by day or by night.
The difference concerns an egg found on the Festival: a chicken lays by day, so an egg found in the morning is permitted.
The Gemara challenges that the nest was examined carefully, so the egg should have been found the evening before.
The egg must have emerged mostly on the eve and returned, following Rabbi Yoḥanan, since once most of it emerged it counts as laid.
A baraita says species with the same intercourse and gestation nurse each other's young; all mate from behind except fish, humans, and snakes.
The Gemara asks what distinguishes fish, humans, and snakes from the other species.
Rav Dimi reports the West says the Divine Presence spoke with them: the fish with Jonah, Adam and prophets, and the snake with Adam.
A tanna taught that a camel mates back to back with its mate.
A baraita lists gestation periods for animals and the trees that correspond to them, from the chicken to the viper and snake.
The Gemara asks from where the seven-year gestation period of the snake is derived.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya, derives it from the curse on the snake, cursed more than all animals and beasts.
The verse's mention of beasts of the field shows the proportion of one to seven, illustrated by the donkey and the cat.
Challenging the derivation, the verse could instead mean one to three, the lion and donkey, yielding nine years for the snake.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara asks whether the verse says cursed from among all beasts, or from among all animals, as the source for the snake's curse.
The verse means the snake is cursed from among the domesticated animals, which are cursed from among the undomesticated animals.
If the snake is cursed in proportion to the donkey, the proportion of goat to cat gives fifteen months, a different result.
Either the verse includes the most accursed animal, the donkey, or the snake receives the most extreme curse the text allows.
The Roman emperor asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya how long a snake's gestation period is.
Rabbi Yehoshua says seven years.
The emperor cites the sages of Athens, who bred snakes and got births after three years.
Those snakes were already pregnant for four years before they were bred.
The emperor objects that snakes mate only to reproduce, that the Athenian sages are wise, and challenges Rabbi Yehoshua to defeat them.
Rabbi Yehoshua asks how many sages there are in Athens.
Rabbi Yehoshua has a sixty-room ship built, buys a butcher's head, and uses reeds to find the entrance to the Athenian school.
Rabbi Yehoshua outwits the guards by reversing his sandal to fake footprints, which leads them to kill their own guards.
Rabbi Yehoshua considers greeting the elders first, since the young sages would otherwise be harmed by the elders.
Rabbi Yehoshua greets the sages of Athens without addressing either group directly.
The sages of Athens ask what Rabbi Yehoshua is doing there.
He replies that he is a sage of the Jews who wants to learn wisdom from them, and they agree to test him.
Rabbi Yehoshua proposes terms: if they win he submits to anything, and if he wins they must eat on his ship.
The sages ask why a man refused a bride would seek a more distinguished family.
Rabbi Yehoshua tries a peg in the lower wall, then the upper hole, showing he may find his destined match in a better family.
The sages ask why a lender would lend again after a borrower failed to repay and the property was repossessed.
Rabbi Yehoshua compares it to someone who cuts reeds by the pond and keeps adding until a passerby helps him lift the bundle.
The sages ask Rabbi Yehoshua to say a matter of nonsense.
He tells of a mule that gave birth with a note claiming 100,000 dinars owed by its father's household.
The sages ask whether a mule can give birth at all.
Rabbi Yehoshua says this is why it is nonsense, since a mule cannot give birth.
The sages ask with what salt is used to preserve it when salt spoils.
He says with the placenta of a mule, and asks whether salt can spoil, rejecting their premise.
The sages ask Rabbi Yehoshua to build them a house in the air of the world.
He pronounces a Divine Name and hovers between sky and earth, asking for bricks and mortar and for the center of the world.
The sages ask who says his claim about the center of the world is correct.
He asks them to bring ropes and measure to verify it.
The sages ask him to bring a pit from the field into the city.
He asks them to braid bran ropes to haul the pit into the city.
The sages ask him to sew together a broken mill.
He asks them to pull threads from the mill and sew them together.
The sages ask with what one harvests a field of knives.
He says with the horn of a donkey, and asks whether a field of knives exists.
The sages ask whether the donkey has a horn, pressing the point about the field of knives.
The sages ask which egg is from a black hen and which from a white hen.
Rabbi Yehoshua brings two cheeses and asks which is from a black goat and which from a white goat.
The sages ask from where the spirit of a chick that dies inside its egg exits.
He says it exits from where it entered.
The sages ask him to show a utensil that is not worth the damage it causes.
He has each sage bring a mat, which cannot pass the gate, so they break the gate: a utensil not worth its damage.
After defeating the sages, Rabbi Yehoshua releases his ship and takes dirt from Athens on the way to Rome.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehoshua fills a jug from the House of the Swallowed and brings the Athenian sages before the emperor, who sees they are suffering.
The emperor objects that these men cannot be the sages of Athens.
Yehoshua throws Athenian soil on them, they regain their arrogance, and the emperor grants him authority over them.
Yehoshua pours the water he brought into a utensil that swallows everything poured into it.
Yehoshua instructs the sages to fill the utensil and go on their way.
The sages pour water repeatedly until their shoulders are dislocated and they are defeated.
Mishna: a firstborn donkey bearing two males gives one lamb to the priest, while a male and female leaves the lamb with the owner.
Mishna: two donkeys each bearing one male, or a male and female, yield two lambs or one lamb to the priest.
Mishna: other combinations of two males and females yield one lamb or nothing for the priest.
Mishna: when only one donkey is a firstborn, the priest receives a lamb for a male, and the owner keeps one for a male and female.
The verse in Exodus 34:20 is cited as the source for redeeming a firstborn donkey with a lamb.
The mishna's rules: any sheep or goat qualifies, the lamb can be redeemed many times, and a retained lamb may be eaten if it dies.
The Gemara asks which tanna taught that twin males of a firstborn donkey yield only one lamb.
Rabbi Yirmeya says the mishna does not follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
If the mishna followed Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, he would hold that simultaneous births are possible, so two lambs would be due.
Abaye replies that the mishna may follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, because a kosher animal differs there.
Abaye cites Exodus 13:12, where the males are the Lord's, to show plural males can both be firstborn.
The Gemara objects that the donkey case should be derived from the kosher animal case.
The Merciful One restricted the rule that two males are firstborn to kosher animals, as the verse shows.
Some say there is another version of the discussion, in which the mishna does not follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
If the mishna followed Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, simultaneous births would make both firstborn.
Abaye replies that the mishna may follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, because a kosher animal differs there.
Exodus 13:12 says the males are the Lord's, which Abaye uses to distinguish kosher animals.
The Gemara asks why the mishna would not teach that both heads emerged as one, if Abaye's reading were correct.
A baraita states that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili gives both twins to the priest, citing the males are the Lord's.
The Gemara objects that the verse concerns the inherent sanctity of a kosher firstborn, not a donkey.
The verse was applied to kosher animals so it serves as the basis for non-kosher firstborn animals too.
The refutation of Abaye is conclusive, so the mishna follows the Rabbis rather than Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

ranges.en: The Gemara asks whether the Rabbis hold that part of the womb sanctifies a firstborn, given that both fetuses cannot be in full contact with the womb.
Rav replies that a substance touching its own kind does not interpose, so each fetus still touches the entire womb.
The mishna: a donkey bearing a male and a female, with uncertain birth order, has the owner designate a lamb to keep for himself.
If the owner keeps the lamb for himself anyway, why does the designation matter?
The designation separates the lamb and removes the donkey's forbidden status.
Since the donkey remains forbidden before designation, deriving benefit from it is prohibited until then.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the mishna follows.
The mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita states that benefit from a firstborn donkey is forbidden per Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Shimon permits it.
The Gemara asks what the reasoning is behind Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Ulla says: is there an item that requires redemption yet is permitted before redemption?
The Gemara objects that a firstborn son requires redemption and is nevertheless permitted.
Ulla means an item the Torah specifically requires redeeming with a lamb, yet it is still permitted before redemption.
The Gemara objects that Rav Nehemya redeemed a firstborn donkey with boiled vegetables of full value, so the lamb is not required.
Ulla refers only to redemption at less than full value, where the Torah insists on a lamb.
Ulla's restated position: the Torah required a lamb to abrogate the forbidden status of the donkey.
The Gemara objects that the second tithe is redeemed with coins, and Rabbi Yehuda permits betrothal with it, implying benefit is permitted.
Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on betrothal with a firstborn donkey applies because the woman knows the donkey will be redeemed with a lamb.
The Gemara asks the reason Rabbi Shimon permits benefit from a firstborn donkey before redemption.
Ulla says: is there an item whose redemption is permitted while the item itself is forbidden?
The Gemara asks whether such a case exists, pointing to Sabbatical Year produce sold for money.
The Sabbatical Year produce's redemption is also forbidden, since the proceeds take on the same consecrated status.
Alternatively, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon dispute the meaning of a verse on shearing and working firstborn animals.
A baraita quotes Deuteronomy 15:19 and 15:19 again, giving the opinions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on what each verse excludes.
The Gemara asks why two verses are needed under each view, and whether Rabbi Yehuda should then forbid benefit from a woman's firstborn son.
Everyone agrees the phrase your ox excludes a woman's firstborn son, and the dispute is over the phrase your flock.
Rabbi Shimon holds that a flock shared with a gentile is exempt from firstborn status, so the verse excludes a firstborn donkey.
The Gemara asks why the verses use both ox and flock if each opinion needs only one term.
Rabba says Rabbi Shimon concedes a firstborn donkey whose neck was broken remains forbidden in benefit.
The Gemara asks the reason for Rabba's ruling.
The reason is a verbal analogy between breaking the neck of the donkey and breaking the neck of the heifer.
Rava asks from where he knows that this is the opinion of Rabbi Shimon.
A baraita lists items susceptible to food impurity despite forbidden consumption, including a firstborn donkey whose neck was broken.
Rabbi Shimon holds none of those items is susceptible to food impurity, and concedes meat cooked with milk is susceptible.
Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Yohanan, derives Rabbi Shimon's view from Leviticus 11:34, where food refers only to what can be fed to others.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If Rabbi Shimon's view holds, why does the baraita specify the time when meat was cooked in milk, since it is food one can feed others?
A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon: meat cooked in milk is forbidden to eat but permitted for benefit, by analogy to the torn animal verse.
The baraita gives two reasons: it is food one can feed others, and even for a Jew it was once fit for eating.
If Rabbi Shimon permits benefit from a donkey after neck-breaking, the tanna should have listed it among items susceptible to impurity.
If the donkey's neck was broken with intent to eat, it is susceptible to impurity; here the breaker had no such intent.
The Gemara asks why the Rabbis deem such meat susceptible to impurity if no one intended to eat it.
The Sages said before Rav Sheshet that its prohibition itself serves as the intent to treat it as food.
If the Rabbis accept that prohibition serves as intent, why does the mishna require explicit intent for an unslaughtered kosher bird carcass?
That mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold that prohibition serves as intent.
Two mishnayot list carcasses and fats requiring intent to become susceptible to impurity, which seems inconsistent with prohibition serving as intent.
Those mishnayot follow Rabbi Shimon, whose own statement elsewhere shows the former clause is not his view.
Rava says everyone, including the Rabbis, agrees prohibition does not serve as intent, so a donkey with broken neck is not susceptible to impurity.

ranges.en: The case is one where the donkey was slaughtered only to train a slaughterer, in the dispute between Nimos and Rabbi Eliezer.
A baraita reports Nimos on a crow slaughtered for practice, and Rabbi Eliezer's view that slaughter blood always renders food impure.
The Gemara asks whether the real difference between Nimos and Rabbi Eliezer is whether prohibition serves as intent for the crow.
The first tanna holds blood renders foods impure in general, but making the crow itself food requires intent to eat it.
Rabbi Eliezer holds even the crow needs no intent, since its prohibition serves as intent; Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis dispute the donkey similarly.
The Gemara asks from where this dispute is inferred.
Perhaps Rabbi Eliezer's view applies because a crow has indicators of a kosher bird, unlike a donkey.
A baraita states that the camel, hare, rock badger and pig are susceptible to impurity because they have indicators of kosher animals.
If kosher indicators are the reason, why do Nimos and Rabbi Eliezer disagree specifically about slaughter for practice?
Even accidental slaughter would count; Nimos holds intentional slaughter for practice still leaves the crow not susceptible to impurity.
The Gemara objects from a baraita that a firstborn donkey whose neck is broken remains forbidden for benefit, against Rabba's view that Rabbi Shimon permits it.
The baraita means benefit is forbidden while the donkey is alive, and Rabbi Shimon may still agree about the dead donkey.
The latter clause refers to benefit while the donkey is alive, so the first clause must not concern living animals.
The latter clause forbids killing the donkey by reed, sickle, ax or saw, or starving it, and forbids shearing and labor per Rabbi Yehuda.
Both clauses concern a living donkey: one bars benefit from its value, the other from benefit from the animal itself, so both disputes must be taught.
Rav Naḥman says Rabba bar Avuh holds Rabbi Shimon concedes it is prohibited to benefit from the donkey after its neck is broken.
Rav Naḥman derives this from Deuteronomy 13:13 with its breaking of the neck, paralleled to the heifer whose neck is broken.
If the tanna is Rabbi Yehuda, the verse seems unnecessary; so is the tanna not Rabbi Shimon?
Rav Sheshet says the tanna is Rabbi Yehuda, and the verse is needed to stop breaking the neck from permitting benefit like redemption does.
Levi's baraita says the owner caused the priest a monetary loss by not redeeming, so the donkey's neck is broken and its benefit forbidden.
If the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, the donkey's value is already lost, so must it follow Rabbi Shimon?
The baraita can follow either Rabbi Yehuda, about the value difference with the lamb, or Rabbi Shimon, about depreciation from death.
Reish Lakish agrees with Rabba that Rabbi Shimon concedes benefit is forbidden after neck-breaking, while Rabbi Yohanan says the dispute remains.
The mishna in Kiddushin, that betrothal with a firstborn donkey is invalid, is cited to support that Rabbi Shimon forbids benefit after neck-breaking.
If the mishna is not Rabbi Shimon's view, whose is it? Rabbi Shimon would validate full betrothal, Rabbi Yehuda only the difference.
Rav says the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda where the donkey is worth exactly a shekel, following Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.
A baraita says redeem immediately for any amount, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says there is no redemption for less than a shekel.
The Gemara asks why the verse needs to teach that redemption is immediate and for any amount, since this seems obvious.
The verse is needed to rule out inferring from the woman's firstborn son, redeemed after thirty days with five sela.
The verse teaches that the donkey must be redeemed immediately and for any amount.
If the verse compares the donkey to a woman's firstborn son, the lamb should be worth five sela; if not, what sets the shekel minimum?
The verse does not compare them; Rava derives from Leviticus 27:25 that every valuation must not be less than a shekel.
The Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda hold that the verse about valuations does not apply here.

ranges.en: Rav Naḥman rules like the Rabbis, so a donkey may be redeemed with a lamb of any value; Rav Yosef adds even a lean lamb worth a ma'a.
Rava supports Rav Yosef from the mishna's statement that the owner may give either a big or a small lamb.
The Gemara asks why this is needed, since it seems obvious that a small lamb suffices.
Lest one think a lamb of little value is not valid, or a lean lamb is unfit, Rav Yosef teaches that either is acceptable.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sent his firstborn donkey to Rabbi Tarfon for redemption.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia asks how much he must give the priest as the lamb's worth.
Rabbi Tarfon cites the Sages: a generous owner uses a sela, a miserly one a shekel, and an average one a ragya.
Rava rules that the halakha is to redeem with a lamb worth at least a ragya.
The Gemara asks how much a ragya is worth.
A ragya is three dinars, between a sela of four dinars and a shekel of two dinars.
The Gemara finds a contradiction between the ragya halakha and Rav Naḥman's any-value halakha.
No contradiction: the ragya applies to one who consults, while any value suffices for one who redeems on his own.
Reish Lakish rules that one lacking a lamb may redeem a donkey with money equal to its value.
The Gemara asks whose opinion this is, since Rabbi Yehuda requires a lamb, so it must follow Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Aḥa teaches the statement as following Rabbi Shimon.
Ravina objects that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, and the unattributed mishna also follows Rabbi Yehuda, not Rabbi Shimon.
Ravina concludes Reish Lakish holds even per Rabbi Yehuda, since consecrated items may be redeemed with any value, and the lamb is a leniency.
Rav Sheizevi says Rav Huna holds that one who redeems another's firstborn donkey acquires the redemption, and the donkey is redeemed.
A dilemma is raised: does the redemption money belong to the redeemer or to the owner?
Per Rabbi Shimon the question is moot since the owner may benefit; per Rabbi Yehuda the donkey is forbidden and belongs to the owner only after redemption.
Is a firstborn donkey like consecrated property, where the redemption money gives title, or is the owner entitled to the difference in value?
A baraita says a thief of another's firstborn donkey pays double to the owner even though the owner has no rights to it now.
If the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, why does the owner lack rights now? It must follow Rabbi Yehuda.
A thief of consecrated property pays no double, and since a thief pays double here, a firstborn donkey is not consecrated.
The mishna: a person with two donkeys, one having given birth before and one not, whose offspring are a male and female with unclear origin.
A baraita asks in what case the lamb enters the pen to be tithed.
It refers to an Israelite with ten donkeys of uncertain firstborn status, who designates lambs and tithes them, since a priest cannot have acquired them.
The baraita supports Rav Naḥman's ruling that an Israelite with ten uncertain donkeys designates lambs and tithes them as his own.
Rav Naḥman rules that an Israelite who inherits certain donkeys or untithed produce from a priest grandfather may separate lambs or teruma as his own.
Both rulings are needed, since separation of produce differs from that of a firstborn donkey, where the lamb comes from elsewhere.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Natan says Rabbi Ḥanina says the same principle applies to one who purchases untithed produce.

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Produce gathered in smoothed piles from a gentile is tithed, but it remains the buyer's, since he owes no teruma or tithes to the priest.
The Gemara asks who smoothed the piles: if a gentile did, the verse about your grain would exclude it from tithing.
A Jew smoothed them while the gentile held them; a gentile cannot acquire land in Eretz Yisrael, so the buyer still owes tithe but not teruma.
A mishna in Demai says produce returned by a Samaritan or unreliable person keeps its tithe and Sabbatical status.
Produce returned by a gentile is treated as gentile produce, but Rabbi Shimon treats it as demai; Rabbi Elazar's disagreement concerns giving it to a priest.
Rav Dimi states Rabbi Elazar's halakha.
Abaye objects: if the exchange were certain, all agree teruma is due, yet Rabbi Shmuel and Rabbi Ḥanina say the buyer owes none.
Abaye cites Rabbi Ḥanina's ruling that the buyer of untithed smoothed-pile produce from a gentile owes no teruma to a priest.
Rav Dimi replies that the mishna concerns teruma gedola, while Rabbi Ḥanina's ruling concerns teruma of the tithe.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from Numbers 18:26 that teruma of the tithe is not owed on untithed produce bought from a gentile.
The mishna states that if the lamb dies, one may derive benefit from it.
The Gemara asks where the lamb died: in the priest's house it is his property, and in the owner's house the benefit is obvious.
Without the rule, one might think the priest has no title until the lamb reaches him; the mishna teaches that it is in his possession from separation.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a firstborn donkey cannot be redeemed with a calf, wild animal, slaughtered or tereifa animal, koy, or uncertain hybrid; Rabbi Eliezer permits a sheep-goat hybrid.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the first clause of the mishna expresses.
It is the opinion of ben Bag Bag.
A baraita of ben Bag Bag derives the exclusions from the Paschal lamb verse, and the repeated redeem phrasing is read to include more animals.
If repetition includes all these animals, the word lamb would serve no purpose; the Gemara asks about ben pekua redemption.
Rav Ashi and Mar Zutra dispute whether a ben pekua, a calf removed alive after its mother's ritual slaughter, may redeem a donkey.
Rav Ashi challenges Mar Zutra: if the Paschal derivation excludes a ben pekua, the repetition of redeem serves no purpose.
A dilemma is raised whether a lamb resembling another animal, with two sheep parents, may redeem a firstborn donkey, and how Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis differ.
A baraita says a cow's offspring resembling a goat cannot redeem, while a ewe's such offspring can.
If that baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, why would it need stating? Is it the Rabbis' opinion?
The baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer; it teaches that the offspring follows its mother, a calf, and cannot redeem.
A baraita of Rabba bar Shmuel defines a hybrid as a ewe's offspring resembling a goat whose father is a lamb.
For what halakha is this baraita stated, sacrifices or something else?
Leviticus 22:27 excludes a hybrid and a resembling animal from sacrifice, and Numbers 18:17 limits firstborn status to a true ox.
The baraita concerns the tithe of animals, or the verbal analogy from under, so resembling animals are not tithed or redeemed.
A dilemma is raised whether disqualified consecrated animals may be used to redeem a firstborn donkey.
According to Rabbi Shimon the question is moot, since the donkey's benefit is permitted and so the lamb is ordinary.
According to Rabbi Yehuda, does a prohibition take effect on another prohibition, or does redemption just cancel the donkey's prohibition?
Rav Mari son of Rav Kahana cites the verse about gazelle and hart, so disqualified consecrated animals cannot redeem a firstborn donkey.

ranges.en: Even per Rabbi Shimon, can disqualified consecrated animals redeem a firstborn donkey, and can a Sabbatical-year purchased animal redeem one?
Redeeming a definite firstborn with a Sabbatical-year animal is forbidden; a doubtful firstborn is not an issue per Rabbi Shimon, who has no doubt.
Per Rabbi Yehuda, does designating a lamb count as consumption, or does the donkey's prohibition make it commerce?
Rav Ḥisda's ruling is cited: a definite firstborn may not be redeemed with Sabbatical animals, but a doubtful one may.
Rav Ḥisda rules that a Sabbatical-year animal is exempt from firstborn status but owes priestly gifts.
The exemption follows from the verse saying for consumption and not for burning, while priestly gifts are for consumption.
A mishna on Sabbatical dough before ḥalla seems to contradict Rav Ḥisda, since the mitzva of ḥalla would then not apply to such dough.
Ḥalla differs, since the verse says throughout your generations, including Sabbatical-year dough.
A baraita derives liability for dough of Sabbatical produce before ḥalla from throughout your generations, which a firstborn lacks.
The Gemara suggests deriving from ḥalla that such an animal does have firstborn status.
With ḥalla the dough is primarily for consumption, but a firstborn's altar portions are primarily for burning.
The mishna: if the owner gave the donkey to a priest, the priest keeps it only after designating a lamb.
A baraita says an Israelite may not give his firstborn donkey to a priest unless the priest redeems it in his presence.
Rav Naḥman says the baraita reflects suspicion of priests, and that every priest may take such a donkey without redeeming it.
Mishna: if a lamb designated for a firstborn donkey dies, Rabbi Eliezer makes the owner liable, but the Sages do not.
Rav Yosef derives Rabbi Eliezer's view from Numbers 18:15, comparing a donkey firstborn to a firstborn man.
Abaye objects: if the donkey may benefit like a firstborn man, why must Rabbi Eliezer bury the dead donkey, unless benefit is forbidden?
Rav Yosef replies the donkey must be buried like a firstborn son, though the Gemara objects that burial is not limited to firstborns.
A baraita: Rabbi Eliezer concedes that an uncertain firstborn donkey's benefit is forbidden until its lamb is designated.
Rava says the verse compares redemption only in regard to the lamb's liability, not to benefit from the donkey.
A mishna states that valuations are fixed at the vow time, and a firstborn donkey is redeemed immediately.
A baraita contradicts this: valuations, nazirite vows, and firstborn redemption do not apply under thirty days.
Rav Naḥman explains that the baraita means that a redemption before thirty days does take effect, but ab initio it is after thirty days.
If Rav said that redeeming a son within thirty days is valid, was that not stated for the firstborn son case?
Rava says everyone agrees that redemption from now on, within thirty days, does not make the son redeemed.

ranges.en: Rav Sheshet holds the firstborn donkey redemption duty begins at birth, so no violation occurs before thirty days.
Rami bar Hama objects with a baraita stating the duty lasts thirty days, after which one must redeem or break the neck.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita's wording implies a mitzva to delay redemption for the full thirty days.
No, the baraita means redemption is a duty throughout the thirty days, and transgression begins only after that.
If so, the baraita should have simply said redeem or transgress, so why mention breaking the neck?
Rava resolves the conflict: the thirty-day baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer's analogy to the firstborn son, while the other follows the Rabbis.
Mishna: one who refuses to redeem breaks the donkey's neck from behind and buries it; redemption precedes breaking the neck.
The mishna supports this ordering with the verse about redeeming the donkey or breaking its neck.
Designating a Hebrew maidservant for her master takes precedence over redeeming her with money.
Exodus 21:8 supports placing the maidservant's designation before her redemption.
Levirate marriage originally preceded halitza, but now that intent is not for the mitzva, halitza takes precedence.
Redeeming a consecrated non-kosher animal belongs first to the owner who consecrated it, ahead of anyone else.
Leviticus 27:27 supports the owner's priority in redeeming a consecrated non-kosher animal.
Chapter-closing formula and the heading of the next chapter, on one who buys a pregnant donkey.
Mishna: one who buys, sells, partners in, or takes a gentile's cow or its fetus is exempt from firstborn obligations.
The verse about sanctifying firstborn in Israel limits the obligation to Jews and excludes others.
Priests and Levites are obligated in firstborn animal sanctity, exempt only from redeeming the firstborn son and donkey.
Why teach the donkey fetus case first, when the cow fetus has inherent sanctity and should logically come first?
Two answers: the donkey case is dear to the tanna per Rabbi Chanina, or the impure-animal matters are brief and set aside.
Reish Lakish, citing Rabbi Oshaya: a Jew buying a gentile's animal with money acquires it and owes firstborn; a gentile buying from a Jew is exempt.
The Master states that a Jew who pays a gentile for an animal, though not pulled, is obligated in firstborn.
What does 'according to their laws' mean? Perhaps it refers to buying gentile persons, inferred from a verse comparing slaves to land.
Leviticus 25:46 compares a gentile slave to ancestral land, acquired by money, deed, or possession, so property should follow a fortiori.
Rejection: if so, property would also be acquired by deed or possession, and Jews buying from Jews shows the inference fails.
Abaye explains 'their laws' as the Torah's prescribed gentile method: property from a gentile is acquired by money, per the counterpart verse.
Objection: the verse may mean nothing at all can be bought from a gentile.
Response: that cannot be, since a fortiori a Jew may buy a gentile's property if he may buy the gentile's person.
Another objection: gentile property may require two acts, pulling and money, as the verse about pulling suggests.
Response: a fortiori from the person being acquired by one act, property too requires only one act.
Further objection: perhaps either act suffices, or the analogy to your counterpart requires both.
Resolution: just as from a Jew property is acquired with one act of pulling, so from a gentile it is one act of money.
Oshaya's statement cited: a gentile who pays a Jew for an animal acquires it without pulling and is exempt from firstborn.
What does 'their laws' mean here? Perhaps the laws of acquiring a Jew's person, inferred a fortiori.
Leviticus 25:51 ties a Hebrew slave's redemption to his purchase money, supporting the a fortiori from a Jew's person.
Rejection: a Jew acquiring from a Jew needs pulling, so acquisition from a Jew's person does not prove acquisition by money.
Abaye's reply: 'their laws' means the acts the Torah prescribed for gentiles, namely money, derived from the counterpart verse.
Objection: the verse may mean a gentile acquires nothing at all from a Jew.
Response: a fortiori, if a gentile can buy a Jew's person, he can buy the Jew's property.
Further objection: perhaps a gentile needs two acts, pulling and money, to acquire from a Jew.
Response: a fortiori from a Jew's person requiring one act, a Jew's property requires only one act.
Final suggestion: a gentile may acquire property by either pulling or paying money, as the counterpart verse suggests.

ranges.en: Restates the principle: property from a counterpart is acquired by one act, pulling, so property from a gentile is acquired by one act, money.
Sets up the Ameimar position: if he holds pulling acquires from gentiles, it follows by Rabbi Yochanan's view that money acquires by Torah law.
If Ameimar follows Reish Lakish, pulling is explicit in the Torah and applies to both Jews and gentiles.
Why then is the phrase 'of your counterpart' needed at all, if both kinds of transaction are effected by pulling?
The phrase does not teach the method of acquisition; it refers to the verse's rule about returning exploitation to one's counterpart.
Suggested inference: one must return exploitation to a Jew but not to a Canaanite gentile slave.
The verse in Leviticus 25:14 is the source being cited for this inference.
Rejection: the exemption from returning exploitation to a gentile comes from 'a man shall not exploit his brother', which does not include gentiles.
Both exclusions are needed: one phrase excludes gentiles and another excludes consecrated property, since each alone would leave the other case unclear.
If the robbery of a gentile is prohibited, the verse is needed to permit keeping exploitation money from gentiles; this works out well.
If Ameimar holds that robbing gentiles is permitted, is it still necessary to state that exploitation from gentiles may be kept?
If Ameimar holds that robbery is permitted, he must hold Rabbi Yochanan's view that money acquires, so the difficulty does not arise.
Objection from a baraita: buying broken gold or silver vessels from gentiles and finding idolatry, the buyer returns it if pulled before paying, but not if after.
If money acquires, why is pulling needed for the Jew to acquire the idol? What case is the baraita dealing with?
The baraita refers to a gentile who accepted that the transaction be adjudicated under Jewish law.
Objection: if so, why is payment of money needed at all? Pulling alone should suffice by Jewish law.
Even with payment, acquisition depends on pulling: if he pulled, he acquired; if not, he did not acquire.
If so, the first clause of the baraita is difficult, since pulling before payment would not effect acquisition.
Abaye explains the first clause: there is a mistaken transaction, as the buyer did not wish to purchase the idol.
Rava objects: if the first clause is a mistaken transaction, the latter clause should also be one, since the buyer does not want the idol in either case.
Rava's resolution: both clauses involve mistaken transactions, but without payment the idol is not seen as held by a Jew, so he may return it.
Abaye replies that the first clause is a mistake because he did not know of the idol, while the latter clause is not, since he paid and should have inspected.
Rav Ashi says the baraita deals with a gentile-law transaction, where pulling does not acquire, so the latter clause also does not.
The word 'pulled' appears in both clauses because the first clause mentioned it to teach that pulling is ineffective, and the latter repeated it.
Ravina says the baraita deals with a Jewish-law transaction, where pulling acquires, so the first clause also has pulling acquire.
The first clause means that if neither money was paid nor pulling done, the buyer returns the item to the seller.
What does 'returns' mean in this context?
It means reneging on a verbal commitment; such reneging is bad faith only between Jews, who are assumed to keep their word, not with gentiles.
