ranges.en: Mishna: animals blemished before consecration have only value-sanctity; once redeemed they count for firstborn and gifts and may be shorn and worked.
Slaughtering them outside is exempt from karet, they do not make substitutes sacred, and if they die they are redeemed and fed to dogs, except firstborn and tithe.
Animals consecrated before their blemish, or blemished after consecration, are exempt from firstborn and gifts and remain sacred for shearing and labor.
Their offspring and milk are forbidden, slaughtering outside incurs karet, they render substitutes sacred, and if they die they must be buried.
The Gemara infers from the mishna's wording that firstborn and gift obligations apply only once the animals were redeemed.
So the tanna holds that value-sanctity defers the firstborn and gift obligations.
Cites the mishna's next clause: the animals leave sanctity for shearing and labor.
If they were not redeemed they remain prohibited for shearing and labor, which supports Rabbi Eliezer's position.
Rabbi Eliezer holds that animals consecrated to Temple maintenance are prohibited for shearing and labor.
Rejection: the mishna need not follow Rabbi Eliezer; the decree applies only to altar animals of value-sanctity, to prevent confusion with inherent sanctity.
Cites the mishna: their offspring and milk are permitted after redemption.
What is the case? If the animal conceived and gave birth after redemption, the offspring are obviously non-sacred.
Rather, the case is conception before redemption and birth after, and the mishna teaches the offspring are still permitted.
Inferring from this, if the animals gave birth before redemption, the offspring remain prohibited until they are redeemed.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Are offspring of value-sanctified animals redeemed while unblemished, or only once they develop a blemish?
Come and hear a baraita: offspring of blemished animals dedicated to the altar may be sold for redemption without a blemish, since their sanctity is subsidiary to the mother's.
The baraita's reasoning: subsidiary sanctity should not be stricter than the primary sanctity, so offspring of a blemished mother cannot be sanctified for the altar.
If one consecrated an unblemished male for its value, it takes sanctity of the body, i.e., inherent sanctity.
This supports Rava, who likewise holds that consecrating a male for its value yields inherent sanctity.
Cites the mishna: one who slaughters such animals outside the Temple courtyard is exempt.
Rabbi Elazar reads the mishna as liability for slaughtering outside, referring to a private altar, and derives the prohibition from a verse.
From where is it derived that one violates a prohibition by sacrificing a blemished animal on a private altar when such altars are permitted?
Deuteronomy 17:1 forbids sacrificing blemished animals; since Leviticus 22:22 covers the public altar, the verse applies to a private altar.
Objection: the verse may instead apply to firstborn, since firstborns are sanctified even blemished, so blemished firstborns should also be offered.
The Sages reply: the firstborn halakha is stated explicitly in Deuteronomy 15, so chapter 17 cannot be referring to firstborns.
Perhaps chapter 17 instead applies to animal tithe, since tithed animals are sacred even blemished and cannot be exchanged, so they too might be offered blemished?
Response: the tithe is excluded by a verbal analogy with the firstborn's passing, so the verse is not needed for tithe.
Objection: perhaps the verse applies to substitutes, which become sacred even blemished under Leviticus 27:10, so they too might be offered blemished.
Response: the substitute halakha is already established, since the verse makes a substitute holy just as the original, so a blemished one is not offered.
Rabbi Zeira objects: perhaps the verse applies to offspring, which are sacred even blemished through their mother, so they too might be offered blemished.
Rava replies that this is already ruled out by another tanna.
School of Rabbi Yishmael: Deuteronomy 12:26 juxtaposes substitutes and offspring with vows, which cannot be offered blemished, so they cannot either.
Cites the mishna: blemished substitutes are not made, i.e., an exchange does not produce a sacred substitute.
What is the reason for this ruling?
The verse forbids exchanging good for bad or bad for good; if bad for good is forbidden, the verse must teach that good renders substitutes sacred and bad does not.
Rather, a good animal from the outset makes a substitute sacred, but a bad one from the outset does not make a substitute sacred.
Cites the mishna: if such animals die, they may be redeemed and fed to dogs.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: this is Rabbi Shimon's view, that altar animals are included in standing and valuation, while Temple-maintenance animals are not.
Rabbi Shimon concedes that an animal blemished from the outset may be redeemed even if consecrated for the altar.
What is the reason for Rabbi Shimon's concession?
Leviticus 27:11 says 'it' is stood before the priest, and the word 'it' excludes an animal blemished from the outset.
The Rabbis hold that for both altar and Temple-maintenance animals, if they die they must be buried.
Whose opinion is the Rabbis' view in the mishna?
It is the school of Levi's view, which holds that all animals, even one blemished from the outset, are included in standing and valuation.
The school of Levi taught in its collection that even a wild animal and a bird are included in standing and valuation.
But isn't 'it' written with an exclusion, which would exclude at least a wild animal or bird? This is difficult for the school of Levi.
According to the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon, is the halakha that dead blemished-from-outset animals are redeemed, derived from 'it'? If so, why did Rav attribute it to Rabbi Shimon?

ranges.en: Since Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis agree a pre-blemished animal can be redeemed, why not state the mishna as Rabbi Shimon's view versus the Rabbis?
Rav follows Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: per the Rabbis, Temple-maintenance animals fall under standing and valuation, altar animals do not, so the mishna cannot follow the Rabbis.
The mishna's latter clause, that altar animals must be buried even if pre-blemished, shows they are included in standing and valuation.
How do we know the burial ruling depends on standing and valuation, rather than on the prohibition of redeeming sacrifices to feed dogs?
If it were the dog-feeding reason, the mishna would also cover a tereifa, which can be stood before the priest; so the reason is standing and valuation.
Alternatively, Rav follows Rabbi Yochanan, who holds the Rabbis include altar animals in standing and valuation, so the mishna fits the Rabbis after all.
Cites the mishna: if their consecration preceded their blemish, they are not counted as sacred for these purposes.
From where are these halakhot derived?
Deuteronomy 12:15 compares disqualified consecrated animals to the gazelle, which is exempt from firstborn, so they are too.
Baraita: exclude such animals from firstborn but not gifts; the verse about the hart excludes them from gifts too, as the hart is exempt from both.
If so, the fat of disqualified consecrated animals should be permitted like that of gazelles and harts, which is not the halakha.
The verse's word 'however' differentiates, limiting the analogy to firstborn and gifts, not to forbidden fat.
The Master said: exclude such animals from firstborn but not from gifts.
What is different about firstborn that only it would be excluded initially, and not the gifts as well?
Firstborn does not apply equally to all animals, only males, while gifts apply to all domesticated animals; so the hart verse is needed to exclude gifts too.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if the analogy holds, why does the baraita not exclude the prohibition of slaughtering an animal and its offspring the same day?
Abaye replies: if compared to non-sacred animals, mother-and-offspring applies; if compared to sacrifices, it applies too, so the verse cannot exclude them.
Rav Pappa counters: by the same reasoning fat should also be unexcluded, yet the baraita derives the fat rule from 'however'.
Abaye's reply: 'however' excludes both fat and mother-and-offspring equally, so disqualified animals are comparable to sacrifices.
Rava says: 'however' excludes mother-and-offspring, and the fat exclusion is derived from the words 'its blood' in the verse about a blemished firstborn.
Deuteronomy 15:23 says only its blood you shall not eat, which Rava uses to derive the fat prohibition.
What does 'its blood' refer to?
If it meant actual blood, the verse would be unnecessary, since all blood is forbidden; so 'its blood' must refer to its fat.
Objection: why did the Merciful One not write 'its fat' directly?
Had it written fat, the juxtaposition and the verse would both apply, excluding karet; so 'its blood' is used to make eating its fat punishable by karet.
Objection: the baraita says 'however' excludes only fat, not mother-and-offspring, so how can Rava take a different source?
Rava explains: without 'its blood' the baraita would exclude fat; the phrase 'its blood' shows mother-and-offspring applies to disqualified consecrated animals.
Cites the mishna: such animals do not emerge from sanctity to become non-sacred for shearing and labor.
From where are these halakhot derived?
Deuteronomy 12:15 permits slaughter, shearing excluded, meat but not milk, and eating but not feeding to dogs; so one may not redeem sacrifices to feed dogs.

ranges.en: An alternative reading: 'you may slaughter and eat' means permission to eat only from slaughter onward, so the dog-feeding prohibition is not derived from 'you may eat'.
Cites the mishna: their offspring and milk are prohibited after their redemption.
What are the circumstances? If the offspring was conceived and born after redemption, why would it be prohibited, since it is like a gazelle's offspring and non-sacred?
Rather, it was conceived before its mother's redemption and born after it, which is why the offspring is prohibited.
If born before the mother's redemption, the offspring is also imbued with inherent sanctity, as the mishna implies by contrast.
From where is it derived that the offspring of a sacrifice is imbued with inherent sanctity?
A baraita derives it from Leviticus 3:1: 'male' includes the offspring of a peace offering and 'female' includes its substitute.
The baraita extends the rule to offspring and substitutes of blemished animals, since 'male' and 'female' include them as well.
What is the status of offspring born after the mother's redemption, which can neither be sacrificed nor redeemed? The Sages disagree on the halakha of those born before.
Rav Huna says: one gathers the offspring into a chamber, where they die of starvation.
They cannot be sacrificed, since their sanctity is deferred from the redeemed mother, and cannot be redeemed, since their sanctity is too weak to transfer to money.
In the name of Rabbi Chanina, in the West: immediately before their redemption, one dedicates them to the same offering as their mother.
Objection: immediately before their redemption implies they are fit to be redeemed, which was established as impossible.
Rather, say immediately before the mother's redemption one dedicates the offspring to the same offering.
What is the reason the offspring are not simply left as they are?
Rabbi Levi: it is a rabbinic decree, lest one raise flocks of them and eventually benefit from them.
Ravina asks Rav Sheshet: according to Rabbi Chanina, may one dedicate the unborn offspring to any offering he desires?
Rav Sheshet answers: no, they may be dedicated only to the offering for which the mother was consecrated.
What is the reason?
By verbal analogy to firstborn animals, which cannot be dedicated to any offering, as Leviticus 27:26 forbids sanctifying the firstborn, so neither can these offspring.
A baraita following Rav Sheshet: redeemed blemish-deferred animals are obligated in firstborn and gifts, and shearing or labor does not incur lashes, before or after redemption.
The baraita continues: before redemption benefit is misuse of consecrated property, offspring born after are non-sacred, and such animals are like non-sacred animals except for valuation.
If consecration preceded the blemish, or a temporary blemish preceded consecration, they are exempt from firstborn and gifts, and shearing incurs lashes and they render substitutes sacred.
The baraita concludes: such animals are like sacrifices in all matters except consumption, and their offspring are sacred and may not be dedicated to any offering.
The phrase 'the principle of the matter' adds cases beyond what one might have excluded, such as slaughtering such an animal outside the courtyard, which is exempt.

ranges.en: The baraita's word 'to include' adds the milk of redeemed disqualified consecrated animals to the prohibition.
The Master said: unblemished offspring of such animals are sacred, cannot be redeemed, and cannot be dedicated to any offering one desires.
Inference: only unblemished offspring cannot be redeemed, so blemished ones can; and only 'any offering' is excluded, so the mother's offering is allowed.
How can both inferences apply together? Is this a refutation of Rav Huna, who holds the offspring must be left to die?
Rav Huna replies that both inferences are false: symmetry of phrasing in the baraita, not a teaching, explains the wording, so no inference follows.
Cites the mishna: one who slaughters such animals outside the Temple courtyard is exempt from karet.
Rav Huna reads the mishna as liability, referring to animals with minor blemishes, following Rabbi Akiva, since they may ascend the altar and not descend.
The baraita continues: before or after redemption, the animal renders its substitute sacred.
Rav Naḥman cites Rabba bar Avuh: the substitute made sacred after redemption must die.
What is the reason?
It cannot be offered, since its sanctity is deferred from the redeemed animal, and cannot be redeemed, since its sanctity cannot transfer to money.
Rav Amram objects: why not let the substitute be eaten in its blemished state by the owners?
As taught in a mishna, the substitutes of firstborn and tithe animals, and their offspring forever, are eaten blemished by the owners.
Abaye replies: a substitute bears its mother's name and takes the halakha of the animal it replaces, so a firstborn's substitute is eaten blemished.
But the substitute of a sacrifice is like a sacrifice: eaten only after redemption, and since its sanctity cannot transfer to money, it cannot be redeemed and so cannot be eaten.
A baraita following Rav Naḥman: the substitute of a disqualified consecrated animal must die, derived from Leviticus 11:4, where 'impure to you' is extraneous.
Objection: the extraneous phrase is needed for the halakha of the five sin offerings that must die.
No; the five sin offerings are derived from the phrase 'of those that have a split hoof is impure'.
A similar baraita: from where is it derived that five sin offerings must die? The verse 'of those that have a split hoof is impure' teaches it.
Objection: the five sin offerings' dying is learned as a halakha passed down by tradition, not from a verse.
Rather, the verse came to teach the substitute of a guilt offering is left to graze.
Further objection: the substitute of a guilt offering is also a tradition, following the principle that where a sin offering dies, a guilt offering grazes.
The verse is needed for the sin offering halakha, and so is the tradition: each alone would leave a different halakha unsettled, such as whether a violation is punished by lashes.
Alternatively, the verse juxtaposes the substitute of cud-chewing animals with the five sin offerings of split-hoofed animals, so both are left to die.
Mishna: one who receives animals from a gentile under a guaranteed investment, with offspring divided between them, begins a new topic.

ranges.en: Mishna: offspring of guaranteed-investment animals are exempt from firstborn for generations, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel extending the exemption to ten generations.
Does the investment still belong to the owner, since he has not yet taken the money owed to him?
Contradiction from a Bava Metzia mishna: a guaranteed investment from a Jew is interest, so the animals stand in the recipient's possession.
Abaye: no difficulty; there the owner accepted responsibility for losses, so the animals remain his, while in the Bava Metzia case he did not.
Rava objects: an arrangement where the owner accepts responsibility is not a guaranteed investment, and the mishna should have distinguished cases.
Rava's resolution: neither case involves accepted responsibility, and the gentile's claim on the offspring means his hand is in the middle, exempting them.
Cites the mishna: if the Jew established the offspring in place of the mothers, the offspring of direct offspring are exempt.
Rav Huna: without establishment, direct offspring are exempt, but offspring of direct offspring are obligated.
Rav Yehuda: offspring of direct offspring are also exempt, and only their later offspring are obligated, as the mishna teaches.
Cites the mishna: offspring of direct offspring are exempt where the Jew established the offspring in place of the mothers.
The Gemara infers that exemption depends on establishment, so without it the exemption would not apply.
This inference conclusively refutes Rav Yehuda's view.
Rav Yehuda replies: the inference is false, since the same holds without establishment, and the mishna teaches only two generations are exempt even with it.
Objection to Rav Huna: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's word 'even' implies both tanna'im agree some generations are exempt, supporting Rav Yehuda.

Asks what the phrase even up to ten generations means on Rav Huna's view

Rav Yehuda replies that the mishna exempts the animals and their offspring

Deuteronomy 22:11 with the analogy to linen, which has not changed
Rav Pappa: all agree such wool is unfit for sky-blue fringe wool
Deuteronomy 22:11-12 with the analogy to linen for the fringe wool

Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: both males are given to the priest

Mishnah: hair shed from a blemished firstborn and stored before slaughter may be used after its death.
Akavya ben Mahalalel permits deriving benefit from the shed hair, a dissenting ruling in the Mishnah.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda reports that the Rabbis prohibit using the wool of a blemished firstborn that shed.
Rabbi Yosei replies that Akavya's leniency was not in the case just mentioned.
Clarified case: shed hair of a blemished firstborn was stored before the animal died; Akavya permits it, the Rabbis forbid.
Wool still attached to a firstborn: if it appears part of the fleece, it is permitted after death; otherwise prohibited.
Objection: Rabbi Yosei's words imply Akavya forbids the wool if the animal was slaughtered, which seems unnecessary to teach.
Rather, the dispute concerns only a dead animal; if it was slaughtered, all agree the wool is permitted.
Reish Lakish explains the dispute: if an expert permitted the animal before shedding, Akavya relaxes the decree; otherwise all forbid.
Objection from a baraita: a blemished animal mixed into a flock forbids the whole group, though Rabbi Yosei says to investigate.
Question: what does Rabbi Yosei mean by saying the matter should be investigated?
Objection: if investigating means removing the blemished animal, the first Tanna would not permit the rest, which is absurd.
Rav Nachman explains the case concerns wool of a blemished firstborn mixed with ordinary wool.
Question: who is the first Tanna who holds all the wool prohibited?
Rabbi Yehuda holds the Rabbis forbid wool if slaughtered, and Rabbi Yosei consistently permits it.
Question: what does 'let it be investigated' mean?
Rav Sheshet objects: investigation tests whether the blemish is permanent, contradicting Reish Lakish's reading.
Rava replies: the investigation checks whether an expert permitted the firstborn before its wool shed.
Ravin brings this halakha from Babylonia and states it before Rabbi Yirmeya.
Rabbi Yirmeya rebukes the Babylonians for teaching such dim rulings, having missed Rabbi Yohanan's explanation.
Rabbi Yohanan's explanation: the dispute concerns a case where one searched and did not find the blemished animal.
The dispute parallels a disagreement between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis.
Mishnah: Rabbi Meir holds impurity persists until located; the Rabbis dig until bedrock or virgin soil.
Rabbi Asi reports a different version of Rabbi Yohanan: the dispute concerns a case where the blemished animal was found.
Baraita on a field with a lost grave: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagree whether to examine the whole field.
Question: why did Rabbi Asi not give Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba's explanation?
Rabbi Asi would answer that a blemish could be temporary and healed, unlike impurity that birds or mice could remove.
Question: why did Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba not give Rabbi Asi's explanation?
Rabbi Hiyya would reply that fields are used for burial, while sacred animals often gore each other, so blemishes commonly develop.
Objection from a baraita: wool plucked from a firstborn that was unblemished stays forbidden even if it later blemished and was slaughtered.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: a blemished firstborn's wool is permitted even without an expert's ruling, contradicting Rabbi Asi.
Reply: the baraita calls the animal unblemished wherever no expert permitted it, even if physically blemished.
Proposal: perhaps Reish Lakish's reading reflects a tannaitic dispute, as the baraita suggests.
Baraita: wool plucked from an unblemished firstborn later blemished is forbidden; Akavya permits wool from a blemished firstborn that died.
Rabbi Yehuda clarifies Akavya's leniency applies to shed hair stored in a compartment before the animal was slaughtered.
Rabbi Yosei reports his father Halafta concedes Akavya in the slaughtered case, while the Rabbis say to place the wool in a compartment.
Objection: if so, Rabbi Yosei matches the first Tanna, so the dispute must concern expert permission instead.
The first Tanna: wool is permitted after slaughter only if an expert permitted the animal before its wool shed.
Rabbi Yosei holds wool is permitted even without prior expert permission, so Reish Lakish's reading is disputed.
Rava replies that all agree on the expert requirement; the disputes concern an animal that died versus one that was slaughtered.
Rava's argument: the first Tanna's three disputes show Akavya's leniency reaches even an animal that died unslaughtered.
Rabbi Yehuda holds all agree wool of a dead firstborn is prohibited; Rabbi Yosei holds all agree it is permitted once slaughtered.
Rav Nachman rules like Rabbi Yehuda, since our mishnah follows his view.
Mishnah: after a blemished firstborn's shed hair was stored and the animal slaughtered, Akavya permits it, while the Rabbis forbid it even after death.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak finds the same ruling in the mishnah's latter clause about dangling wool.
Objection: the dangling-wool ruling cannot fit either Rabbi Yosei or Akavya under the slaughter or death readings.
Rather, the clause follows Rabbi Yehuda, which is obvious.
Question: in what case does this ruling apply, if the animal died?
Rather, it refers to slaughter, so Akavya and the Rabbis disagree in the slaughter case; the Gemara concludes accordingly.
Rabbi Yannai asks whether plucking wool from an unblemished burnt offering is permitted, or wool torn out by itself.
Reply: there is no dilemma for sin or guilt offerings, or firstborn and tithe animals; the real question concerns burnt offerings.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Dilemma: is a burnt offering kept longer than needed, given that it also atones, making its wool prohibited?
Baraita: wool plucked from an unblemished firstborn is forbidden, so wool torn out by other means is permitted; a burnt offering is easier.
Rejection: even wool torn out by other means is forbidden; the baraita speaks of plucking to show Akavya's far-reaching view.
Question: the Mishnah speaks of wool shed naturally, so why does the baraita speak of plucking?
Mishnah, abbreviated: wool dangling from a firstborn that was not completely shed.
Question: what does it mean for dangling wool not to appear to be part of the fleece?
Reish Lakish: strands whose root points upward count; Rav Natan bar Oshaya: strands not compressed with the fleece count.
Question: why did Reish Lakish not adopt Rav Natan bar Oshaya's more straightforward explanation?
Rabbi Ile'a: fleece cannot be sheared without dangling hairs, and Rav Natan's reading would forbid all such fleece.
Chapter-closing formula for 'The one who buys an animal', followed by the start of the next chapter.
Mishnah: Israelites must tend a firstborn thirty days if small, or fifty days if large, before giving it to the priest.
Rabbi Yosei says three months for small animals; a priest asking for it within that period may not receive it.
A blemished firstborn may be given to a priest to eat; an unblemished one, in Temple times, may be given to be sacrificed.
Mishnah: a firstborn is eaten year by year; if a blemish arises within the year, it may be kept twelve months, otherwise only thirty days.
Question: from where are these waiting periods derived?
Rav Kahana derives the periods from Exodus 22:28-29, which juxtaposes firstborn sons with sheep and oxen.
Objection: the verses could be read in reverse, giving thirty days for oxen and fifty days for sheep.
Rava: the extra 'you shall do' for oxen adds further care, and the exact fifty-day period was given to the Sages.
Baraita on the same verses: 'you shall do' adds an extra act for oxen, and the exact period was given to the Sages.
The Sages set the periods; Rabbi Yosei's three months reflects the extensive effort needed to raise small animals with tiny teeth.
Mishnah: if the priest asks for the firstborn within that period, the owner may not give it to him.
Question: what is the reason the owner may not give the firstborn to such a priest?
Rav Sheshet: such a priest resembles one who assists at the threshing floor for teruma, so the arrangement is prohibited.
Baraita: priests, Levites, and poor people assisting in barns or slaughterhouses may not receive teruma or tithe as wages; doing so desecrates it.
Scripture cited: Malachi 2:8 on corrupting the covenant of Levi, and Numbers 18:32 on not desecrating sacred items.
Question: why cite a second verse, if the first only indicates desecration without a death penalty?
The second verse, Numbers 18:32, indicates that desecrating sacred items carries the penalty of death.
The Sages wished to penalize such givers and require full teruma separation, but refrained lest people mistakenly separate from exempt produce.
Baraita conclusion: all these cases carry the same prohibition against giving teruma or tithe as wages.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Heading: owners of produce enjoy a benefit of discretion in choosing which priest or Levite receives teruma and tithes.
Baraita example: a non-priest may hand teruma to a designated priest for a coin, but a priest may not pay for priestly gifts.
Question: why does the baraita mention only teruma and not the priestly gifts, which also allow the owner's discretion?
Teruma has inherent sanctity and cannot be redeemed, so a priest will not treat it as ordinary; priestly gifts have monetary sanctity and could be wrongly treated as redeemable.
Rava: teruma from outside Eretz Yisrael is not subject to the assisting-priest prohibition; Rav Chama gave such teruma as wages to a priest servant.
Shmuel: outside-Israel teruma is nullified by a majority; Rabba nullified it and ate it while impure, acts forbidden for Eretz Yisrael teruma.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua nullified outside-Israel teruma wine in a vat, drawing one jug at a time to drink, then continuing with each new batch.
Shmuel: outside-Israel teruma need not be separated before eating; one may eat first and separate afterward.
Shmuel: outside-Israel teruma is forbidden only to one impure from his own body, not from contact with corpses; touching it is permitted.
Ravina: a menstruating woman may separate challah abroad; a minor priest eats it, or it is burned and re-separated to keep the category remembered.
Narrative: Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rami bar Chama are traveling by ferry when a woman poses a halakhic question.
The woman asks whether one impure from a corpse may immerse and then eat outside-Israel teruma.
Rav Nachman begins answering the woman's question, addressing Rami bar Chama.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: since there is no sprinkling of ashes, how can immersion help a person who touched a corpse?
Rami bar Ḥama replies that they should wait for Rav Naḥman rather than answer now.
Rav Amram reports Rav's ruling that one made impure by a corpse may immerse and eat teruma outside the Land.
Rejects Rav's ruling: the halakha does not follow him.
Mar Zutra cites Rav Sheshet with a parallel ruling on creeping-animal impurity to support the rejection.
Rejects Rav Sheshet's ruling as well: the halakha does not follow him.
The Mishna teaches that a firstborn is eaten year by year, whether or not it developed a blemish.
The Gemara infers from the Mishna's wording that the firstborn's year is counted from its own birth.
Asks from where this principle about counting the year is derived.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav's teaching that the verse in Deuteronomy supplies the derivation.
The verse about eating the firstborn before the Lord year by year supports counting the animal's own year.
Asks which year is meant when one year enters another.
The year meant is the firstborn's own year, not the calendar year.
The school of Rav taught eating for one day this year and one day the next, two days and a night in total.
Asks from where the school of Rav derives that rule for firstborns and for sacrifices generally.
Rav Aḥa bar Yaakov answers by citing the Leviticus verse about a lamb in its first year.
The lamb's own year in that verse is its birth year, not a count of years since creation.
Asks from where Rav derives that a firstborn is eaten for two days and one night.
Rav derives it from a verse in Numbers, as the answer to the question.
The verse juxtaposes the firstborn with the peace-offering breast and thigh, so the same two days and one night apply.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why cannot the verse about the firstborn be read as deriving the two-day rule directly?
Such a derivation would instead compare the firstborn to the breast and thigh of a thanks offering, eaten one day.
Asks how Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, responds to that objection.
The extra 'yours' in the verse adds a second, distinct firstborn ruling, extending the eating period to an extra day.
Asks how the school of Rav responds to the same inference.
The phrase 'it shall be yours' teaches that a blemished firstborn is given to the priest, a rule not found elsewhere in the Torah.
Rav Yehuda derives from the plural 'their flesh' that the rule covers both unblemished and blemished firstborns.
Asks how the school of Rav would answer that derivation.
The plural refers to the firstborns of all Israelites, not specifically to blemished animals.
The Mishna teaches that a blemish within the first year allows keeping the animal for twelve months.
Poses a dilemma: does the rule cover thirty extra days after the first year, or do the two cases differ?
A baraita about firstborns in the present era states the owner may keep a blemished animal within the first year, with thirty days allowed.
Raises a further doubt: are the thirty days counted after the year or before it?
A baraita on a blemish within fifteen days supports R. Elazar, who grants thirty days counted from when the blemish appeared.
Some say R. Elazar teaches thirty days after the firstborn's year when a blemish appears within that year.
The verse 'before the Lord your God you shall eat it year by year' is cited as the source.
Asks which days are reckoned as a year for this purpose.
The days reckoned as a year are these thirty days.
Objects with a baraita stating that a blemish within fifteen days is completed to fifteen days after the year.
Replies on whether the fifteen-day completion baraita refutes R. Elazar; the terse reply is disputed.
The Mishna teaches: R. Yehuda permits a firstborn slaughtered after its blemish is shown, while R. Meir forbids it unless an expert does so.
Rabbah bar bar Ḥana explains that all agree on the rule for experts' checks; the dispute is only about bodily blemishes.
Explains that R. Meir decrees bodily blemishes as analogous to expert checks, while R. Yehuda does not.
A baraita states R. Yehuda's view that expert-checked blemishes are forbidden because they change, while bodily blemishes are permitted.
Objects: would bodily blemishes be thought to change at all, rather than the changes coming from the expert checks?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's position is introduced to resolve the matter.

ranges.en: The Gemara infers from the Mishna's wording that R. Meir penalizes a non-expert by forbidding the animal.
Poses a dilemma about whether all corneal blemishes change after death, and asks its practical difference for witnesses.
Resolves the dilemma by a baraita in which R. Yoshiya offers to show corneas that change, implying some do not.
The Mishna teaches that a non-expert who had the animal slaughtered on his ruling buries it and pays from his own property.
Asks whether the anonymous Mishna follows R. Meir, or refers only to corneal blemishes where all agree.
A baraita teaches that the compensation is one quarter of a small animal's value and half of a large animal's value.
Asks what the reason is for the difference between the sheep and the bull.
R. Pappa explains that the loss from the bull is great while the loss from a small animal is slight.
Objects that if so, he should pay in proportion to the actual loss.
Rav Huna bar Manoaḥ reports Rav Aḥa's reply that the Sages fixed one quarter to discourage raising small livestock in the Land.
The Mishna teaches that a judge who errs pays damages from his own funds, unless he was an expert serving the court.
Asks whether the Mishna follows R. Meir, who holds liability for indirect damage, as the judge's case.
Rav's case: a judge who took and gave by hand an item that caused the loss, making him liable.
Notes that the case of a judge finding the innocent party liable is clear when the judge took and gave the item by hand.
Asks how the case of a judge exempting the liable party works, if the judge said the defendant is exempt.
Objects that the defendant did not take and give by hand, so the case cannot be that one.
Rabina offers examples: a judge who had a pledge taken from him, and cases of making pure items impure or impure items pure.
Recounts the episode where R. Tarfon fed a cow to dogs, the sages at Yavneh permitted it, and Todos the physician explained the rule.
R. Tarfon states his ruling on the matter in the case of the cow's owner.
R. Akiva rebukes R. Tarfon: as an expert serving the court, he is exempt from paying compensation.
Objects: why not derive the exemption directly from a case of error in a Mishna?
Explains the two distinct points the Mishna makes, that an error about a Mishna is corrected and that the judge is then responsible.
Offers an alternative: the judge erred in judgment rather than in a Mishna, so the expert is exempt from paying.
The Mishna teaches that one who takes payment to inspect firstborns may not slaughter on his ruling unless he is an expert.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages in Yavne permitted Ila to take a fixed fee for examining small and large firstborns, paid whether or not they were blemished.
Asks why the fee for examining a large firstborn is higher than for a small one.
Restates the Mishna's clause that the fee is paid whether the firstborn is unblemished or blemished.
Asks why the examiner is paid for an unblemished animal, when a blemished one is explained by his permitting it.
Otherwise people would suspect him of declaring a blemished animal unblemished, so the fee is paid either way.
Objects that the same suspicion arises in reverse, since he could declare an unblemished animal blemished to collect the fee twice.
Replies that the Sages allowed one fee per firstborn, so he has no incentive to misdeclare it.
The Mishna teaches that wages void rulings, testimony, and the sprinkling or sanctifying of the red heifer waters, and lists exceptions for priests and elders.
Asks from where the principle that judges may not take payment for rulings is derived.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, derives it from the verse in Deuteronomy about Moses teaching statutes for free.
A baraita adds that one may learn for pay only if no free teacher is available, citing Proverbs to forbid selling truth.
The Mishna teaches that water and ashes of a red heifer taken for pay have the status of cave water and burnt ashes.
Objects with a Mishna saying that betrothal with red heifer water or ashes is valid even for an Israelite.
Abaye reconciles the two: one Mishna concerns sprinkling and the other concerns the rite of betrothal, so no contradiction.
Quotes the Mishna clause that a priest made impure by the requester is supplied from his teruma.
Asks how the examiner himself may go to the bet hapras, given that the Sages had ruled against such pay.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says that a person may walk through a bet hapras, a rabbinic ruling about its status.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yehuda bar Ami relays Rav Yehuda that a trodden beit hapras is pure, so a priest is only concerned about other impurities.
Repeats the Mishna clause about an elderly examiner carried on a donkey, and explains that he is paid as an idle laborer would be.
The Mishna teaches that one may not buy meat, untanned hides, or bleached wool from a suspect examiner, while R. Eliezer permits female hides.
Explains that deer meat is forbidden because it could be confused with calf meat.
Infers from the Mishna that tanned hides may be bought, since a firstborn's hide would not be tanned with such effort.
Gives the reason: he would not take that trouble on a firstborn's hide, fearing the Sages would confiscate it.
States R. Eliezer's view that hides of female animals may be bought from the suspect person.
The reason is that people know the difference between male and female hides by their anatomy.
Asks why the first tanna forbids female hides if they are sold, given that R. Eliezer permits them.
The first tanna fears a man would pass off male hides as female, claiming mice ate the part, which R. Eliezer finds easy to detect.
The Mishna teaches that one may not buy bleached or dirty wool from the suspect person.
Asks why the Mishna must teach dirty wool, since bleached wool is already excluded.
The Mishna is teaching a single case: wool that was both bleached and cleaned of its dirt.
The Mishna teaches that spun thread and garments may be bought from the suspect person.
Asks why garments need teaching, since spun thread is already permitted.
Garments here means felt garments, which are not made of spun thread.
The Mishna on the Sabbatical Year: flax, even combed, may not be bought, but spun thread and woven fabric may.
Asks why woven fabric must be taught, since spun thread is already permitted.
Woven refers to wool woven into chains, which is not spun.
The Mishna on the suspect of selling teruma as non-sacred produce: one may not buy even water and salt, per R. Yehuda and R. Shimon.
Asks what the Mishna comes to include with the word about the suspect's wares.
Offers an example: the case of a suspect butcher who mixed fish entrails with olive oil, showing what is included.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava penalized a butcher who sold forbidden kidney fat as permitted intestinal fat, and banned him from selling even nuts.
Rav Pappa asks Rava which Mishna opinion his ruling follows, suggesting it must be R. Yehuda's.
If Rava follows R. Yehuda, the butcher should be barred from selling even water and salt, which is absurd.
Rava answers he follows R. Shimon, penalizing only items tied to the prohibition, and gives an example of misleading butchers' children with nuts.
The Mishna teaches that suspicion about one of Sabbatical or tithe produce is separate, while impure-food suspicion may cover both, and a suspect may not judge or testify on that matter.
Asks why one suspect about the Sabbatical Year is not suspect about tithes.
Tithes are treated more strictly since they must be eaten within Jerusalem's walls, so the seller is careful about them.
The Mishna's second clause: one suspect about tithes is not suspect about the Sabbatical Year.
Asks why one suspect about tithes is not suspect about the Sabbatical Year.
Tithes can be redeemed so they are treated lightly, whereas Sabbatical produce is always forbidden and so is treated more strictly.
The Mishna teaches that one suspect about either the Sabbatical Year or tithes is suspect about selling impure food as pure.
If suspect in Torah-law matters, all the more so in rabbinic matters such as purity of non-sacred food.
The Mishna teaches that some are suspect about purity but not about Sabbatical produce or tithes.
Asks why one can be suspect about rabbinic prohibitions but not about Torah-law ones.
Raises a baraita: trust in purity implies trust in Sabbatical produce, and so suspicion in purity implies suspicion in Sabbatical produce.
Rabbi Ilai and Rabbi Yannai offer answers: a man seen practicing stringencies privately, or one who accepted both observances before the Sages.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana relays Rabbi Yoḥanan that the anonymous Mishna is R. Akiva's view, while the Sages hold that suspicion about the Sabbatical Year is separate.
Asks who the Sages are in this dispute.
Identifies R. Yehuda's local view that the Sabbatical Year is stringent, illustrated by a man who cursed his neighbor's wish to eat Sabbatical fruit.
A variant attribution gives the same R. Akiva and Sages positions, with the Sages' view stated as suspicion over tithes and Sabbatical Year.
States the Sages' view that one suspect about tithes is suspect about the Sabbatical Year.
Asks who these Sages are.
These are R. Meir, who holds that one suspect in one matter is suspect in the entire Torah.
R. Yona and R. Yirmeyah, students of R. Zeira, relate a variant attribution, stating the Sages hold suspicion about the Sabbatical Year is a separate matter.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the earlier position that one suspect about tithes is suspect as to what the sages hold.
Asks who the sages are in the first view.
They are R. Yehuda, whose locale treated Sabbatical produce stringently.
The opposing view: one suspect about tithes is suspect about the Sabbatical Year.
Asks who the sages are in the opposing view.
They are R. Meir.
A baraita: an am ha'aretz who accepted fellowship rules is suspect in all of Torah after one failure, per R. Meir, while the sages limit it.
A baraita on a convert who accepted fellowship rules, treated as an Israelite, with a practical difference for the validity of his marriage.
A baraita: a gentile who seeks to accept fellowship rules, or words of Torah beyond one matter, is not accepted.
R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda widens this to even one legal detail, citing a verse that a priest denying a rite has no share in priesthood.
A baraita: if one practices purity privately, he is accepted, then taught, otherwise taught first and then accepted.
R. Shimon ben Yoḥai holds that he is accepted either way and learns in his own manner.
A baraita: one is accepted for wings first, then for purity; if he accepts only wings, he is not accepted for purity either.
A baraita states that Beit Shammai accept a convert for liquids for thirty days and for twelve months, while Beit Hillel accept each for twelve months.
Argues that if Beit Hillel held twelve months for both, Beit Shammai would be lenient, so Beit Hillel must mean thirty days for both.
A mnemonic of letter codes is given to recall the rulings listed.
A baraita: one who accepts fellowship rules must do so before three fellows, but a fellow's sons and household need not.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the sons and household too must accept before three fellows, since they are not like a fellow.
A baraita: a scholar must accept before three fellows, but an elder who sits in the academy need not, since he accepted from the time he sat.
Abba Shaul holds that even a scholar need not accept before three fellows, since others accept on his behalf.
R. Yoḥanan recalls that in the days of R. Hanina ben Antigonus's son this Mishna was taught, with R. Yehuda and R. Yosi involved.
A question arose about purity matters, so the sages sent to R. Hanina's son.
The sages sent to examine him found him handling purity matters, and he stood by his own review.
R. Yehuda says his father despised scholars, and so he too despises them.
R. Yosi replies that an elder's honor should stand, and since the Temple's destruction priests have treated purity matters with self-importance.
A baraita: a fellow whose wife, sons, and household have died remains in his status, and a dyed-blue courtyard is presumed valid until disqualified.
A baraita: a woman or daughter of an am ha'aretz who marries a fellow, or his slave, must first accept fellowship rules.
Conversely, a fellow's wife, daughter, or slave who marries an am ha'aretz need not first accept fellowship rules.
R. Meir says even these must accept fellowship rules at the outset.
R. Shimon ben Elazar relays R. Meir: a woman who married a fellow and sewed phylacteries for him, then married an am ha'aretz and tied his customs-officer knots, illustrates the point.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: am ha'aretz who retracted from fellowship practices is never readmitted, per R. Meir.
R. Yehuda distinguishes: retraction in private means no readmission, but public retraction allows it.
Another version: readmission depends on whether the person had acted as a fellow in private at the outset.
R. Shimon and R. Yehoshua ben Korḥa readmit in both cases, citing Jeremiah's call to backsliding children to return.
R. Yitzḥak of Akko reports R. Yoḥanan's ruling that the halakha follows that pair, so returnees are readmitted in both cases.
A baraita: formerly a fellow who became a tax collector was rejected from fellowship, even after resigning.
Later sages hold that one who resigns from tax collection is like any other person and may be readmitted.
Narrative: the sages needed Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya, who had become a tax collector, and Rabba went to him while Rav Yosef did not.
Rav Yosef cites the earlier baraita rejecting readmission, and Rabba cites the later baraita allowing it, as the basis of each choice.
A baraita: a person may inspect all firstborns except his own, but may inspect his own consecrated animals, tithes, and purity.
Asks what the baraita's case is, since it says a person may inspect all firstborns except his own.
Objects: a single person cannot be trusted with such a ruling, so it must be a court of three, and a judge in such a case is not suspect.
Replies the case is a single expert, and a single expert may rule on others' firstborns but not his own, given his vested interest.
Chapter closing formula asking how far Israelites are liable, marking the end of the chapter.
The Mishna teaches that disqualified consecrated animals' benefit goes to the Temple, and firstborns and tithes are sold in the butcher shop and weighed.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the Mishna: benefit from selling disqualified consecrated animals goes to the Temple treasury.
Asks when this applies, since after redemption the benefit would belong to the owner.
Rejects that reading: after redemption the animal is the owner's, so the benefit is his.
Objects that the animal cannot be slaughtered before redemption, because redemption requires standing and valuation first.
Analyzes which view on standing and valuation for altar animals would make the Mishna's slaughter workable.
Asks what can be said if altar animals are included in standing and valuation.
The Mishna refers to the redemption itself: the Temple gains by pressing owners to redeem at higher prices.
The Mishna excludes the firstborn and animal tithe, whose benefit belongs to the owner.
Asks why a firstborn is not sold in a butcher shop while a tithe might be sold at home.
Brings a baraita on firstborns and tithes as a contrast to the proposed distinction.
Narrates that Rav Sheshet found this difficulty both at night and again at dawn from the baraita.
Resolves it: the tithe concerns an orphan's animal, and the sale is motivated by returning lost property.
Narrates how R. Idi reported a teaching to Rav Sheshet, who became angry and dismissed it.
Asks what Rav Sheshet derived from the matter.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, derives a point from the verse 'I will dwell in your tent forever'.
Explains that David meant the words of teaching will be spoken in this world, citing R. Yoḥanan in the name of R. Shimon ben Yoḥai.
R. Yoḥanan states that the lips of a sage who speaks a teaching move in the grave.
R. Yitzḥak bar Zeiri cites the verse about the sleepers' lips moving, interpreting it as the same point about sages.
A baraita: an orphan's tithe animal is sold, and a slaughtered tithe animal's tithe is absorbed in its hide, fat, sinews, and horns.
Asks what the baraita means.
Abaye explains that the orphan's tithe is sold by absorption, implying an adult's would not be sold that way.
Asks how this differs from a baraita on a lulav bought in the Sabbatical Year.
A baraita: one who buys a lulav from another in the Sabbatical Year gives an etrog as a gift, since he may not buy it.
Asks what happens if the seller does not want to give the etrog as a gift.
Rav Huna says the price of the etrog is absorbed in the lulav, since that case is clear, while the case here is not.
Rava objects: if so, why would the tithe be sold twice, once as a sale and once absorbed?
Rava explains the baraita: the orphan's tithe is sold as usual, and the adult's tithe is absorbed in its parts.
Rava cites a verse about a substitute being holy and not redeemed, showing that substitution applies before slaughter.
The Rabbis decreed that a substitute after slaughter applies as before slaughter, lest it be taken as a live animal.

ranges.en: Rava's principle, adopted by Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak: the Sages did not decree on items not valued during life, so the orphan's tithe may be sold.
A verse about eating meat after slaughter, with the blessing, is read as showing that the animal tithe's meat is sold only after slaughter.
Poses a dilemma: may the value of the meat be included in the cost of the bones?
R. Ḥiyya and R. Shimon ben R. Yehuda HaNasi dispute this, one permitting and one forbidding inclusion of bones.
They do not disagree: one speaks of a small animal whose bones are unsaleable, the other of a large one.
Alternatively both speak of a large animal, and each follows his own locale's custom regarding bones.
Returning to the baraita: a firstborn may not be redeemed or sold, while a tithe is not redeemed, and so not sold alive or slaughtered.
Asks where these rules are derived from.
R. Yoḥanan derives from the verse that tithe may not be redeemed, linking it to the devoted items through the phrase about sale.
R. Naḥman bar Yitzḥak tells Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua the reason the verse is phrased this way.
Objects: if the reason were not that, one could argue devoted items apply to everything, so the verse is needed for some other purpose.
Derives that devoted items cannot be redeemed by analogy to tithe, which is holy before and after, with an objection noted.
Derives the same rule by analogy to the firstborn, which is holy and not redeemed, with an objection about why the verse is needed.
Derives transfer by analogy to the firstborn, whose holiness comes from the womb, with the objection that the verse is needed for exclusion.
Pursues the firstborn analogy for tithe as well, arguing the verse about tithe is needed to exclude.
Objects that the tithe's exclusion is still open to the same challenge, so the verse about transfer is superfluous.
Proposes deriving firstborn redemption from devoted items via the redemption term, and the reverse, asking which derivation is valid.
Asks what practical difference this makes.
Cites a teaching of R. Yishmael's school: return and coming back, applied where there is no comparable case, while a comparison is used where one exists.
Where a comparison exists, the firstborn transfer is derived from tithe, and devoted items are contrasted with tithe and firstborn in the verse's exclusions.
Rava says the verse about not being redeemed is unnecessary for devoted items, depending on whether they belong to the owners or to the priest.
A baraita: devoted items while in the owner's house are holy for all purposes, and once given to the priest they are like non-sacred items for all purposes.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects: if the verse's redemption wording is not about devoted items, apply it to tithe; but then the firstborn could be meant, and the reply rejects that.
Rav Ashi derives from the verse that a tithe and its substitute are holy and not redeemed, so the prohibition concerns selling.
Rav Ashi argues that redemption cannot apply while alive, since standing and valuation are needed, so the verse must mean the animal may not be sold.
Objects: this works only if altar animals are included in standing and valuation, while the other view would read the verse literally.
Explains that the verse cannot be read literally, since no animal is redeemable only after slaughter and not while alive.
Asks why it cannot be said that the animal is redeemable after slaughter, since its sanctity then weakens.
Rejects that reasoning with an a fortiori argument: a living tithe's strong sanctity still bars redemption, so the slaughtered one cannot be redeemed either.
Asks why the Merciful One did not simply write that the animal may not be sold.
Had it written sold, one would think only selling is barred and redemption allowed, so the verse says not redeemed to cover both.
The Mishna: Beit Shammai hold an Israelite may not be counted with priests for a blemished firstborn, while Beit Hillel permit it even for a gentile.
Identifies the Mishna's view as that of R. Akiva.
A baraita: a firstborn is counted only by a group of priests, per Beit Shammai, while Beit Hillel and R. Akiva permit even gentiles.
Beit Shammai's reason is a verse that the meat is for priests, and as priests alone may eat there, so Israelites are excluded.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Beit Hillel reply that the rule about the pure and impure eating together is about a blemished firstborn, which is written explicitly.
Beit Hillel's a fortiori inference: an impure priest may eat a blemished firstborn, so a non-priest, who may eat lesser sacred meat, certainly may.
Objects that an impure priest is special, since the impure may serve in communal service when pure priests are absent, so the inference fails.
Beit Hillel reply that the a fortiori argument concerns eating, not service, and a non-priest's eating outranks an impure priest's.
R. Akiva's reason from the verse about gazelle and deer: as gentiles may eat these, so too disqualified firstborns may be eaten by gentiles.
Asks what the other tanna, who rejects R. Akiva's view of Beit Hillel, relies on.
The verse's three mentions of gazelle and deer each teach a distinct rule, including that disqualified consecrated animals are exempt from firstborn status.
A baraita: Beit Shammai forbid giving a blemished firstborn to menstruating women, while Beit Hillel permit it.
Asks what Beit Shammai's reason is.
Beit Shammai reason from the verse comparing firstborn meat to the breast and thigh of the wave offering, which impure people may not eat.
Beit Hillel reply that the comparison applies only to the unblemished firstborn, since the verse explicitly lets the impure eat the blemished one.
Beit Shammai answer that the permission for impure eating applies only where impurity does not emerge from the body itself.
Beit Shammai cite a Mishna: the Passover offering brought in impurity may not be eaten by those with bodily impurity, showing the Torah distinguishes these cases.
Beit Hillel reply that the verse about impure persons is specific to the defiled-by-corpse case, while the verse here is general.
A baraita: one may not accustom others to firstborns, or to disqualified consecrated animals, on a festival.
Asks why a festival is treated differently when the animal is not fit to eat, and which tanna holds the firstborn rule.
Rav Ḥisda says it is Beit Shammai who hold that one may not feed a menstruant or disqualified consecrated animals.
Asks which tanna this is.
It is R. Elazar son of R. Shimon, from the Mishna on two sin offerings, one blemished and one whole.
The Mishna: of two sin offerings, the whole one is offered and the blemished one redeemed; if the blemished one is slaughtered, the whole one's blood decides its fate.
R. Elazar son of R. Shimon holds that even if the meat was cooked, the whole offering is forbidden once its blood was sprinkled.
Rav Ḥisda explains the whole Beit Shammai position as applying only to firstborns, whose holiness comes from the womb, not to disqualified consecrated animals.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Suggests reading the whole baraita as R. Elazar son of R. Shimon's view, so that firstborns and other animals are treated alike.
R. Elazar may hold that other disqualified animals keep sanctity because it can transfer to redemption money, but a firstborn's sanctity cannot.
Objects: R. Elazar agrees that disqualified animals are sold by weight, so why does he forbid skinning a firstborn from the feet, which is also profitable?
Resolutions: the hide's gain is offset by flesh loss, skinning resembles sacrificial work, or it is a decree against holding herds of disqualified animals.
The Mishna: a firstborn that is bled, even if dying, may not be bled, per R. Yehuda, while the sages allow it if no blemish is made.
A baraita: a firstborn may be bled where no blemish is made, and not where one is made, per R. Meir, while the sages allow even where blemish is made.
R. Shimon and R. Yehuda give further views on whether it may be slaughtered after the blemish, and on bleeding a dying firstborn.
R. Elazar taught his son, or R. Ḥiyya did, that these disputes match the dispute about a teruma jar with a doubt of impurity.
R. Eliezer, R. Yehoshua, and Rabban Gamliel each state how to handle the jar, with R. Meir following R. Eliezer and the sages following R. Yehoshua.
Asks how we know R. Meir's view is limited to the case where one acts directly.
R. Meir's view is limited to acts done by hand, while the case here is indirect, where R. Yehoshua's view applies.
R. Eliezer's view applies to the jar only because Elijah might come and purify it, while the sages hold the indirect case alike.
R. Yehuda holds the direct-act limit as in the jar case, while the indirect case follows R. Yehoshua.
Rabban Gamliel distinguishes the case where Elijah might purify it from the case where letting it be leads to death, where the sages agree.
Adds that the two sides also dispute by different verses, so the cases are not identical.
R. Yoḥanan states that all agree on leaven and on the one who maims, and cites verses about crushing and severing to show what is liable.
Explains the dispute: R. Meir reads that no blemish should be in it, while the sages read the verse about a whole animal as being for acceptance.
The sages cite the verse requiring a whole animal for acceptance, and R. Meir reads the same verse.
Asks what R. Meir does with the verse about wholeness, if a blemish from birth is obvious, and proposes it excludes disqualified animals after redemption.
Explains the sages' concern: if disqualified animals are forbidden for shearing, then blemish is forbidden too, so the rule is taught.
A baraita reads the verse no blemish shall be in it as applying to indirect blemish, so direct-action blemishes are also covered.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita's rule: one may not give a firstborn a blemish, even indirectly.
Derives the indirect case from the verse 'there shall be no blemish in it', which covers any blemish, including one caused by a dog.
Reports that the teaching disputes verses: R. Eliezer reads the plural terumot as covering both pure and uncertain teruma, while R. Yehoshua reads it as singular.
Asks whether R. Eliezer holds that the vocalization of the Torah is authoritative.
A baraita on a Hebrew maidservant reads bevigdo as garment, which contradicts R. Eliezer's reading of the spelling.
States R. Akiva's view and R. Eliezer's reading that the spelling bevagdo is authoritative, creating the conflict.
Resolves: the dispute is over whether teruma not fit for you must be safeguarded, with R. Eliezer holding Elijah may purify it.
Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's ruling that the halakha follows R. Shimon.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak objects: which R. Shimon, since Shmuel already taught that an unintended act is permitted, and conflicting reports attribute rulings to Rav and Shmuel.
Shmuel means R. Shimon in the baraita, that one may let blood of a firstborn, as stated explicitly.
The Mishna: one who pierces a firstborn's ear may never slaughter it, per R. Eliezer, while the sages allow slaughter if another blemish arises.
Asks whether R. Eliezer always penalizes, and raises a contradiction from a baraita about one with a skin affliction.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Mishna: one who excised a leprous mark is purified by a new mark per R. Eliezer, while the sages require the new mark to spread over the whole body or shrink.
Rabba and Rav Yosef reply that R. Eliezer penalizes indefinitely only in property matters like the firstborn, since one would otherwise risk blemishing it.
Rava objects that R. Eliezer's view here conflicts with his view in Nega'im, while the sages are consistent across the two.
Resolves both views: the sages penalized the transgressor for the specific act, so the penalty tracks what he did, consistently across both mishnayot.
Rav Pappa asks whether the Mishna reads yit'har or veyit'har, which changes whether the first mark's impurity persists.
Asks what practical difference the wording makes, given the impurity from the second mark anyway.
The Mishna: a bridegroom who sees a leprous mark is given seven days of celebration, and on a festival, the whole festival.
Explains the wording's consequence: under one reading the first mark is purified and the seven days kept, under the other the first mark remains.
Records a dilemma R. Yirmeyah brought to R. Zeira, left unresolved.
Asks whether one who pierced a firstborn's ear and then died may be penalized through his son, by analogy to other cases.
Objects with analogies: the one who arranged labor on a festival is not penalized, and the sons might be penalized for property, but the man is absent.
Asks whether the sages penalized him over his property or for the sake of the son.
A baraita: a field cut in the Sabbatical Year and sown after it, and the sages penalized the owner's son, as proof of property penalty.
Rav Asi bar Ḥanina says we hold that if one improved the field and died, his son sows it, which establishes the penalty on the property.
Abaye concludes that the sages penalized the father's property but not the son himself, and so we hold this.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If someone rendered another's pure items impure and died, the sages did not penalize his son after him.
Asks what the reason is.
Damage that is not visible is not damage under Torah law, so only a rabbinic penalty falls on the man, not his son.
The Mishna: a Roman official slit the ear of an old firstborn ram, then of others; the sages permitted the first, then forbade the rest.
The Mishna: children tied lambs' tails, one tail was severed and sages permitted it, then others tied tails and were forbidden; intentional blemish forbids, unintentional permits.
Explains why the children incident is needed: a minor might develop a habit, unlike a gentile, so the rule must cover both.
R. Ḥisda cites Rav: the permission applies only if he said to make a blemish, while an outright act is treated as a blemish made directly.
Rava objects: whether it occurs or is made, a blemish is caused without intent in the same way, so Rav's distinction makes no difference.
States the principle: whatever is done intentionally is forbidden, and unintentional cases are permitted.
Asks what the word about including means in the principle.
Includes an indirect cause, and includes one who does not intend the blemish, like one who passes by with his rushing.
The Mishna: a firstborn chased and kicked, thereby blemished, may be slaughtered.
R. Pappa limits this to a kick during the chase, not after it, which is obviously so.
Asks whether this is because the animal remembers the pain, so that the teaching is needed.
A variant: even after the chase, the reason is that the animal remembers its pain, so the same rule applies.
R. Yehuda holds it is permitted to blemish a firstborn before it emerges into the world.
Rava's example of a kid and a lamb with blemished ears, and whether eating without visible harm still constitutes a blemish.
Asks what the Mishna is teaching with this example.
The Mishna teaches about outer and inner strings that were chipped or uprooted, which are blemishes.
Asks the reason uprooted strings are blemishes, and suggests it is because they show when the animal bleats.
Rav Pappa and Rava hold the Mishna itself explains the reason: uprooting is a blemish because it shows when the animal bleats.
The Mishna: shepherds who are Israelites are trusted for blemishes, but priest shepherds are not, with varied rulings by R. Shimon ben Gamliel and R. Meir.
R. Yoḥanan and R. Elazar debate which shepherds are trusted, with one holding priests are trusted for drink but not for Israelite flocks.
Explains that the trusted person might give the animal to another when burdened, and the same reasoning applies priest to priest.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds one is trusted about another's animal but not about his own.
R. Meir holds that one suspect in a matter is not trusted to judge or testify on it.
Another view holds that Israelite shepherds and priest shepherds are both trusted.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the rule: a priest's Israelite shepherd would not be trusted, since he might be bribed with a taste of the firstborn.
Sets out the positions: R. Shimon ben Gamliel trusts a priest-shepherd for another's firstborn but not his own, and R. Meir bars suspect people from testifying even for others.
Asks what R. Meir adds on each reading of the shepherd cases, since the view it contradicts is already implied.
Shows the dispute is with R. Yehoshua ben Kefusai, who requires two independent witnesses from the marketplace for a firstborn in a priest's house.
The baraita continues: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows even a priest's son or daughter, and R. Yosei excludes household members even among ten.
Asks whose opinion underlies Rav Ḥisda's ruling, citing Rav Ketina, that an uncertain firstborn born to an Israelite requires two outside witnesses.
Rav Naḥman says the owners may testify, arguing from the tithe animal, which can also be blemished, and asks whether R. Meir allows that testimony.
Objects: if you say no one can testify about the firstborn because there is no remedy, then the same applies to the owner.
Cites a Mishna in which R. Yosei holds that a priest whose animal is in the hands of a priest is exempt from gifts, while R. Meir holds him liable.
Concludes that owners may testify, since it is priests who are suspected of blemishing, while Israelites are not suspected of blemishing.
Reports that Rav Naḥman rules like R. Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rava rules like R. Yosei.
Objects that Rava himself said owners standing outside may testify about an animal that enters whole and exits injured.
Objects: if all owners may testify without suspicion, what is the teaching for, and why is there a need for this statement at all?
The halakha follows R. Shimon ben Gamliel, but only for a son or daughter, not a wife, since a wife is regarded as the husband's own body.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if R. Meir holds a suspect in one matter is suspect in all of Torah, does the same apply to priests not judging cases?
Objects that the verse 'by their word shall every dispute and every affliction be decided' implies priests should judge, contradicting the rule.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Meir's suspicion of priests means only that they might have caused a blemish, not that they definitely did.
Raises a dilemma: is hearsay testimony admissible for a blemished firstborn?
Rav Asi forbids slaughter on hearsay testimony for a firstborn, while Rav Ashi permits it.
Rav Asi objects with a school of Menashe baraita: hearsay is valid only for a woman's testimony that her husband died.
Rav Ashi emends the baraita: hearsay is valid wherever a woman's testimony is valid, which includes firstborn blemishes.
Rav Yeimar accepts hearsay for firstborn blemishes, and the halakha is that hearsay is valid in that case.
Rabbi Ile'a: a priest who says an animal is a firstborn with an unintentional blemish is believed, and the expert may permit it.
Asks whether this is the principle that the mouth which forbade is the mouth which permitted, citing the Ketubot case of a divorcee's claim.
Distinguishes: a woman can refrain from speaking, but for firstborn animals the blemish is visible and eating it would be obvious, so the rule is needed.
Objects: what is the difference from a case of someone who hired a donkey to a friend and was dishonest?
Recounts the donkey case: the hirer was told to avoid the river route, went by the river, and the donkey died, and he then claimed a route with no water.
Rava and Abaye: what would the hirer gain by lying, and in a case of doubt rather than eyewitnesses one does not reason that way, since the blemish is evident.
Recounts Rabbinis' statement without a witness and Rava's transmission from R. Ile'a about R. Tzadok and his firstborn barley-fed animal.
Story: a man's firstborn with split hoof came to R. Yehoshua, and asked whether they distinguish between an Israelite and an am ha'aretz.
R. Gamliel says the same story, that R. Yehoshua recognized the authority of R. Gamliel's claim.
R. Yehoshua is told to stand up while witnesses testify against him.
R. Yehoshua stands and argues that the living cannot refute the dead, and the crowd rebukes the interpreter until he is silenced.
The Mishna: a priest may testify that he saw this firstborn, and that it has a blemish.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, explains: a priest may testify that a Israelite gave him the firstborn with a blemish, since such things are not likely to be lied about.
Rav Ashi: the same logic applies to the Mishna, since it is only the sacrifices outside that are not eaten, but where suspicion exists, the priest is suspected.
Rav objects: why not reason that such things are not lied about, when one suspected in tithes cannot be trusted, distinguishing that case?

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The agent could evade the accusation by claiming he trusted the seller.
The latter clause of the Mishnah supports this: from so-and-so, he is trusted.
There, with a claimant present, the agent is afraid to lie.
R. Yirmeya asks from where Yehuda derives this ruling.
The case is one where the animal grew in the owner's own possession.
Yehuda rules an Israelite is trusted to say he gave a blemished firstborn to a priest.
Objects that the point is obvious and needs no teaching.
What is the law for a minor who grew up?
The ruling is needed so one does not think the earlier establishment fails.
Sura and Pumbedita taught the two versions differently, and the halakha follows the first.
Rafram in Pumbedita gave a firstborn to a priest unblemished, then blemished it himself.
Later the animal was brought before him for judgment.
The priest claims an Israelite gave him the blemished firstborn, and the claim is exposed.
Rafram objects that he himself gave the animal to the priest, exposing the false claim.
Still he did not care, since that man was brazen and others are not.
A man brings a blemished firstborn to Rav Ashi, arguing the owner's status is irrelevant.
Ravina objects that the owner may be an Israelite, so the ruling would not apply.
Rav Yehuda says a firstborn of an Israelite is not inspected unless a priest is with it.
Rav Ashi distinguishes the case with a priestly-food analogy, upholding Rav Yehuda.
Since the blemish is evident, why was the matter brought before the Sages?
Offers an explanation tied to honoring a sage's dignity.
Mishnah: everyone is trusted about the blemishes of tithe animals.
Why are they trusted, since one could blemish it from the start unseen?
Raises an objection about exposing the animal before ten men.
Leviticus 27:33, he shall not inspect between good and bad, supports the rule.
The verse's concern is that one could blemish his whole flock.
Mishnah: a blinded, maimed or broken firstborn is slaughtered on three Israelites' word; R. Yossi requires an expert.
Teachings attributed to R. Shimlai and R. Yehuda Nesia permit a firstborn outside the Land on three men's word.
Rava asks what this teaches if the case concerns only evident blemishes.
Cites the Mishnah on the blinded firstborn as a source.
The Mishnah's evident-blemish wording shows R. Yossi's authority, not a broader rule.
R. Yehuda cites R. Yirmeya b. Abba on a doubtful tradition from Rav and Shmuel: three permit a firstborn without an expert.
What new rule does this teach about a firstborn with no expert present?
Cites the Mishnah that a firstborn is slaughtered on three men's word.
Permitted where no expert exists, but not where one is available.
Rav Chiya bar Amram: three permit a firstborn or a vow where there is no expert or sage.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The teaching excludes R. Yossi's view and R. Yehuda's view on three permitting vows where no sage exists.
A baraita is cited: three annul vows, but R. Yehuda requires one of them to be a sage where none exists.
Asks who holds this view.
Rav Nachman identifies himself as an example of the case.
R. Yehuda's wording implies the other two need not be sages.
Ravina says it is reasonable that R. Yehuda holds this position.
R. Yossi holds the ruling applies even when a High Priest is present.
Rav Hananel reports Rav's ruling that halakha does not follow R. Yossi.
Objects that this is obvious, since halakha follows the majority over the individual.
Clarifies the ruling is taught so that one does not think his reasoning stands.
Proposes settling the matter from an earlier teaching said in Samuel's name, with the other implied.
Mishnah: if a firstborn or cow was sold as unfit, the seller refunds the money, with rules on who keeps what was eaten.
Baraita: a seller of meat, produce or wine later found to be firstborn, tevel or libation wine refunds the price.
R. Shimon b. Elazar: refund in full where the soul abhors the item, but deduct the value where it does not.
Lists items the soul abhors, such as carrion and creeping things, and items it does not, such as firstborn and tevel.
Asks why the buyer does not simply say what the seller ruined for him.
The case is one where the buyer purchased from a place with a known blemish.
The seller explains that had the buyer not eaten, he could have shown the animal and it would have been permitted.
Gives an example following R. Yehuda on tevel, and eating libation wine through mixture.
Cites the Mishnah on libation wine in a cistern, with Rabban Shimon b. Gamliel's ruling, as support.
Mishnah: which blemishes allow slaughter of a firstborn, such as a torn or cut ear, and what counts as dry, per R. Yossi b. HaMeshulam.
Asks why the verse is needed, since lame and blind are written in Deuteronomy.
Notes that the verse also says if it has a blemish, bringing a second textual basis.
Objects that the general phrase is limited to the specific cases of lame and blind, so nothing else applies.
Replies that a general-specific-general structure limits the rule to what resembles the specific case.
Derives that visible blemishes that do not return apply generally, following the specific pattern.
Proposes an alternative reading: visible blemishes that disable work and do not return apply generally.
Asks why the Mishnah specifies damage to the cartilage of the ear and not to the skin.
Explains that every bad blemish is an inclusive expansion.
If so, asks why the Mishnah does not also teach hidden blemishes.
Cites the Mishnah on outer threads damaged and inner threads uprooted as the source for the hidden-blemish case.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the Mishnah does not also teach a temporary blemish, if the rule extends beyond the listed cases.
Argues a temporary blemish is a reasonable extension, but leaves the question unresolved.
We do slaughter on this point, as a baraita teaches.
Cites Leviticus 27:11 on an unclean animal that may not be offered.
Asks whether the verse speaks of blemished animals that were redeemed, or of a truly unclean animal.
Concludes from the separate mention of unclean that the verse concerns blemished animals that were redeemed.
Objects that one might think they may be redeemed for a temporary blemish.
The verse excludes an animal never fit to offer, while a temporarily blemished one is offerable tomorrow.
Objects: if so, why do we need the lame and blind cases at all?
Quotes the Mishnah: a cracked animal is unfit even if no part is missing.
Baraita: a crack or damage counts whether caused by people or by heaven, enough for a fingernail to catch.
Baraita: a perforated ear is unfit at the size of a lentil, and R. Yossi b. R. Yehuda says a bean.
What counts as dry: pierced without a drop of blood, and R. Yossi b. HaMeshulam says enough to fold.
Asks which views the tanna equates, and whose words they are.
The first tanna and R. Yossi b. R. Yehuda agree on a bean as the minimum.
Brings a contradicting baraita on the awl and how other tools are included by the verse.
