Quotes R. Yossi b. R. Yehuda: any item taken in hand is included.
Rabbi says: just as the awl is a special metal tool, so all metal tools are included.
R. Yudan reports Rabbi's teaching on piercing with an awl, and the Sages' view on a priest made blemished.
Asks how a priest became blemished if piercing only happens at the top of the ear.
Rav Hana b. Katina: no contradiction, since one case is about slaughter and the other about disqualification.
Asks whether a lentil-sized opening means one going in and out, or one standing still.
Rav Huna says he has not heard this exact ruling, but has heard something similar in the Mishnah.
Cites the Mishnah on a missing spine or skull and whether it conveys impurity in a tent.
Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute the measure of a missing vertebra and of a skull opening.
Rav Chisda asks how much of a removal from a living animal makes it die.
Rav Tachlifa b. Abudimi says Samuel ruled the amount is like a sela.
Reports conflicting attributions: Rav Safra calls it a tradition, while Rav Shmuel b. Yehuda calls it a Mishnah.
Points to Rav Shmuel b. Yehuda as the source of the teaching.
Objects that this would make the disputes of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel identical.
Mishnah: a hole not made by human hands is measured as a large fist, the size of a melon-seller's fist.
R. Yossi says a hole made by human hands is measured as the size of a large borer in a chamber.
Compares the measure to an Italian coin and a Nironit sela.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Opens the discussion of a hole in a yoke, and the speaker falls silent.
Rav Chisda asks whether the taught case is perhaps a borer with a plug.
Rav Tachlifa rejects the perhaps: it is certain that a borer with a plug must hang, as Hezekiah ruled.
Invokes Hezekiah ben Akash, as the Mishnah teaches, to support the ruling.
Hezekiah's testimony before Rabban Gamliel at Yavne: a vessel lacking an inside or back for smoothing, with its impurity rules for earthenware.
The Torah ties impurity to having an inside: with an inside it becomes impure, without one it does not.
R. Yitzhak b. Avin restates the rule for wooden vessels by analogy to earthenware.
Asks why the rule must be hung on earthenware, when it could be stated for wooden vessels.
It teaches that a vessel with an inside is like an earthenware vessel.
Argues by analogy that wooden vessels follow earthenware in impurity of inside and back.
Grants that the Torah reveals the inside of earthenware, but asks whether it reveals the inside of wooden vessels.
Resolves that the case concerns rabbinic impurity of liquids, not Torah impurity.
Cites a Mishnah on a vessel impure at its back by liquids, with its basin, ear and hands clean.
Explains the Sages' decree on liquid impurity of a zav or zava, and why they made it like earthenware for recognition.
If so, asks why a vessel without an inside should not also be marked for recognition.
Since the mark was made for vessels with an inside, the rabbinic status of those without one is known.
Draws an analogy to a sack: a portable item that is full or empty, like the vessels fit for treading.
If so, asks whether earthenware also cannot transmit treading impurity.
Rav Pappa says the Mishnah's large borer implies a simple borer, by inference.
Zutra asks whether the same holds for a sela, and what the Rabbis can say when R. Meir's view works.
Cites the Mishnah: a small borer of physicians is R. Meir's view, and the Sages require a large borer of the chamber.
Objects that R. Meir's view would make him lenient like Beit Shammai and stringent like Beit Hillel.
Asks what our own Mishnah teaches, and whether it teaches or does not teach the point.
Rav Nachman rules on the measure as a Nironit sela, equal to a large borer.
Mishnah: blemishes of the eye, including pierced, damaged or cracked eyes, and what counts as a blemish in the white and the black.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the term harisa means in the eye blemish list.
Rav Pappa explains it as a thin tavlul, a bull-like eye film.
A baraita: a thin sunk spot is a blemish, but a floating one is not.
Objects that the opposite is taught elsewhere.
No difficulty: one case concerns black, the other white.
Resolves the conflict by a black case and a white case, with thin spots in each.
Report from Yoshiyah of Usha: thin black sunk is a blemish, thin white floating is a blemish, with a mnemonic.
Raises whether the snail is the snake, or perhaps the snake is a different creature.
Cites a report of an old man who taught that a snail is a fixed blemish, the snake the Sages mention.
Though a person does not inspect his own blemish, a scholar teaches students who then teach him.
Objects with Rav Huna's ruling: a scholar who taught before the act is heeded, otherwise not.
Asks what is a white tavlul: one that cuts the sira.
Attributes the Mishnah to R. Yossi, as taught in a baraita.
Baraita: white entering black is a blemish per R. Meir; R. Yossi holds black entering white is not a blemish.
Rav says there are no blemishes in white.
Grounds R. Yossi's view in the verse, their eyes bulge from fat, where eye fat is called eyes.
Explains R. Meir's view: tavlul is what confuses the eyes.
Mishnah: a chorvor and standing water as blemishes, with R. Hananya b. Antigonus's three-check rule.
Attributes the view to R. Yehuda, as taught in a baraita.
Baraita: chorvor forty days and standing water eighty days, per R. Meir.
R. Yehuda: chorvor eighty days, and irrigation water eaten wet and dry requires three months.
Objects that both versions are taught here, so a word must be missing from the text.
Baraita: wet and dry from rain is a blemish, from irrigation not; eaten dry then wet is no blemish until dry after wet, over three months.
Objects: really? But it was taught otherwise.
Rav Idi b. Avin reports Rav Yitzhak b. Ashian: Adar and Nisan are wet, Elul and Tishri dry, and the halakha is refined by halves.
Raises whether wet-and-dry is judged by the wet season or the dry season.
Cites the report on Adar and Nisan, arguing that Elul and Tishri fruits are fed to the animal in those months.
Asks how much is fed to the animal in the proof.
R. Yohanan in the name of R. Pinchas b. Arouba: the amount is the size of a fig, and Rava notes the question in the West.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how many feedings count, whether every meal or the first one, and whether before or after eating.
Asks whether a blemish is judged before or after drinking, noting the earlier case that benefits after drinking.
Asks whether a tied animal or a loose one counts, noting that the loose one certainly benefits.
Asks whether the animal is alone or with its companion.
Asks whether the case is in the city or in the field.
Rav Ashi asks about a garden adjacent to the city, and the question is left undecided.
R. Chanina b. Antigonus cites Rav Nachman b. Yitzhak that the cure must be three times; Pinchas asks Shmuel's view.
If he ate and was not cured, is the blemish retroactive or from now on, and what changes for redemption?
Samuel expounds a verse, Isaiah 33:23, as the source for a word in the discussion.
Mishnah: a pierced, damaged or cracked nose or lip is a blemish.
Baraita: a nostril pierced from outside is a blemish, from inside not; a lip pierced, damaged or cracked is a blemish.
Rav Pappa explains the term bull as a lip.
Mishnah: outer threads damaged or crushed, inner ones uprooted; R. Chanina b. Antigonus says do not check the tiyumet inward.
Baraita on what counts as tiyumet, and whether slaughter is for outer parts only, per R. Yehoshua b. Kapuchai.
R. Chanina b. Antigonus says we do not heed the tiyumet at all.
Asks what R. Chanina b. Antigonus means.
R. Yehoshua b. Kapuchai is the first tanna, and the text is missing words that the reading supplies.
Defines inner parts from the tiyumet inward: applies to damaged or crushed, but uprooted may be slaughtered.
R. Yehoshua b. Kapuchai: slaughter only on the outer parts; inner uprooted parts do not permit slaughter but do disqualify.
R. Chanina b. Antigonus: do not heed the tiyumet at all, not even to disqualify.
Rav Ahadboy b. Ami asks whether a limb missing from within counts as missing.
Cites verses: lame or blind for firstborns, blind or broken for sacred animals, to ask which applies to disqualification.
Asks whether the disqualification question for blemish is what the verse means.
Cites Leviticus 22:21, that the animal must be perfect for acceptance.
The Merciful says perfect, meaning no lack.
Asks whether perfect includes all blemish, so that a lack from the outside also disqualifies.
Cites Leviticus 7:4 and a baraita on the kidneys: one kidney is included and three kidneys excluded.
Explores whether the dispute is whether internal lack counts as lack.
Rav Chiya b. Yosef: all agree a creature with one kidney exists, and internal lack counts as lack.
No difficulty: the case is resolved by the earlier distinction.
Here it was created with two and lost one; there it was created with one from the start.
Objects that the teaching is parallel to the case of three.
Explains the parallel: three from the start, so one from the start, unless the creature exists from the beginning.
The sources dispute whether a creature with one kidney exists; R. Yohanan says all agree it does not, and internal lack counts.
No difficulty: the case concerns an animal lacking in one part.
Here the lack is before slaughter, there after slaughter, and after slaughter before acceptance.
Asks who permits the animal in that case.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects with Rav's ruling that one who pierces a bull's ear and then receives its blood is disqualified.
Cites Leviticus 16:14 on taking from the blood of the bull.
Asks who permits the bull when it was blemished before receiving, after receiving, or before sprinkling.
A baraita from Exodus 12:5 requires a perfect, year-old lamb at slaughter, receiving and sprinkling, and R. Yehoshua's view on the blood-sprinkled sacrifices.
Rava: this shows that blemishes at these stages disqualify sacrifices.
Asks whether this is a dispute between tannaim.
Cites Leviticus 22:24 and R. Yehuda's view that the blemishes apply to testicles and not to sinew.
Proposes that R. Yehuda also applies it to testicles, and R. Eliezer b. Yaakov and R. Yossi differ on crushing and cutting.
Asks whether the dispute is simply over whether internal lack counts as lack.
One view holds internal lack counts as lack, the other holds it does not.
Asks what R. Yossi holds on this point.
Explains the positions: the dispute concerns visible blemishes, since cutting and crushing are treated differently.
R. Yehuda: crushing and contracting are blemishes, and cutting and removal are blemishes since they hang.
R. Eliezer b. Yaakov: crushing is not a blemish since it was sometimes whole, and neither is removal.
R. Yossi: crushing is a blemish because it is absent, and cutting is not since it is present.
Mishnah: a damaged tail, ear or lip for sacred animals, and a bone or flesh loss of a finger's width.
R. Elazar and a baraita: damage without removal of a scrotum or male organ, plus R. Yossi b. HaMeshulam's story of a wolf that took and returned a part.
Asks what halakha depends on a finger being one of four in a handbreadth of every person.
Rabbah says it applies to the matter of tekhelet.
Baraita on tekhelet threads: Beit Shammai say four, Beit Hillel say three, and the other measure of a handbreadth.
R. Huna b. R. Yehoshua: the measure is two cubits, as the Mishnah teaches.

40a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Describes the two cubit-length measuring sticks kept in the Temple chamber and how much longer each is than Moses' cubit.
The mishna asks why there were two cubit measures, one large and one small.
The purpose: artisans took payment by the small cubit and returned work by the large one, avoiding misuse of consecrated funds.
The Gemara asks why two large cubits are needed at all.
One large cubit measured silver and gold with a small difference; the other measured wood and stone construction.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak, or alternatively Rav Huna bar Natan, ties the baraita's fingerbreadth to the mishna's flesh-between-joints measure.
The mishna states that a firstborn with no testicles, or only one, may be slaughtered.
Rabbi Yishmael holds that two scrotal sacs indicate two testicles, so a single sac counts as one testicle.
Rabbi Akiva says the animal is seated on its rump and the sac is pressed to see whether a testicle emerges.
An incident: pressing failed to bring out a testicle, it was later found attached near the loins, and Rabbi Akiva permitted it.
Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri prohibited that animal, disagreeing with Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara asks why the mishna mentions no testicles at all if having one is already a blemish.
The mishna is incomplete; it should teach that two testicles in one sac, or two sacs with one testicle, is a blemish.
Restates Rabbi Yishmael: an animal known to have two testicles but only one sac is treated as having just one.
Rabbi Akiva's position: even a known case is not accepted on that basis; one must press the sac.
A baraita reports a Piran incident: a testicle failed to emerge, it was found attached, and Akiva and Yohanan ben Nuri disagreed.
Rabbi Akiva objects that Yohanan ben Nuri is wrongly destroying Israelite property by forbidding such animals.
Yohanan ben Nuri retorts that Akiva is feeding Israel carcasses by permitting animals that should not be eaten.
The Gemara asks how Yohanan could call them carcasses, since properly slaughtered animals are not carcasses.
Suggests Yohanan meant animals with wounds that will kill them within twelve months, i.e. tereifot.
Objects that the prohibition is not about tereifot, so this explanation does not fit.
Offers a revised reading: Yohanan meant Akiva feeds sacrifices outside the Temple, since such an animal is an unblemished offering.
The mishna lists animals with five legs, three legs, closed hooves, or a shahul or kasul as blemishes permitting slaughter.
The mishna asks what a shahul is.
A shahul has a dislocated thighbone; a kasul has one thigh set higher than the other.
Rav Huna: a missing or extra hind leg is a tereifa too, since an extra limb counts as a removed one.
Rav Pappa: round hooves count as a blemish even if they are also split, not only when wholly donkey-like.
Introduces a baraita on the terms kasul and shahul.
The baraita asks what a kasul is and what a shahul is.
A shahul has a dislocated thighbone; a kasul has one leg inside the loin and another dislodged above it.
Another baraita: saru'a is one thigh longer than the other, and kalut has closed hooves like a donkey's or a horse's.
Mishna: a broken foreleg or hind-leg bone is a blemish even if not conspicuous; Ila listed these in Yavne and the Sages deferred.
Ila added three further blemishes beyond the standard list.
The Sages reply that they never heard of these three blemishes.
Ila answers with the three: a round human-like eye, a pig-like mouth, and most of the speaking part of the tongue removed.
The court that followed them ruled that each of these three counts as a blemish permitting the firstborn's slaughter.
If a broken bone is not conspicuous, the Gemara asks, is it really a blemish at all?
Rav Pappa: not conspicuous in its own form, but conspicuous through its function, meaning how the animal walks.
Recalls Ila's blemish list and its enumeration.
The Gemara asks whether a round eye is a blemish because such eyes are not the normal form for animals.
Raises a contradiction from a Nidda mishna on the impurity of a miscarried animal-form fetus judged by sex, including Rabbi Meir's view.
Rabba bar bar Hana cites Rabbi Yohanan on the matter, leading into the question of Rabbi Meir's reasoning.
Asks the reason for Rabbi Meir's ruling.
Because the eye is round like a human's, a miscarried fetus of that kind is impure.
Rav Yosef: no contradiction; one Nidda case refers to the black of the eye, the other to the white.
The baraita lists a pig-like mouth as the next blemish.
Rav Pappa: a pig-like mouth is a blemish when the upper lip overlaps the lower, even if the mouth is not pointed.
Quotes the mishna clause that removal of most of the speaking part of the tongue is a blemish.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the tongue clause in the mishna reflects.
It is the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita supports this by stating Rabbi Yehuda's view that most of the speaking tongue must be removed to be a blemish.
The mishna recounts an incident where the lower jaw protruded beyond the upper jaw.
Rabban Gamliel asks the Sages for a ruling on that jaw case.
The Sages rule that such a protruding lower jaw is a blemish.
The Gemara asks why the mishna presents this as an incident rather than as a rule.
Because an earlier mishna already taught the pig-like mouth, this incident is presented as the disputed case.
Notes that the Sages disagree with Rabbi on the pig-like mouth ruling, and the Gemara specifies the scope of that dispute.
The disagreement concerns an upper lip overhanging the lower; when the lower overhangs the upper, it is a blemish regardless.

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the mishna's incident: the lower jaw of a firstborn protruded beyond the upper jaw.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel asks the Sages for a ruling on that jaw case.
The Sages rule that such a protruding jaw is a blemish permitting the firstborn's slaughter.
Objects that the mishna on lips protruding is taught about people, so it need not apply to animals.
Cites the verse on men of Aaron's seed, showing that the lip rule about priests concerns only people.
Concludes that since the verse speaks only of people, a lower lip protruding in an animal should not be a blemish.
Rav Pappa: the mishna means a lower jaw with a longer bone, which is a blemish even in animals; the other case lacks a bone.
The Sages' view: a doubled kid ear is a blemish only if the extra ear has its own bone.
Rabbi Hananya ben Gamliel: a kid's tail resembling a pig's, or with fewer than three joints, is a blemish.
A baraita distinguishes swelling from wind, which is no blemish, from swelling due to a large bone, which is one, and ears similarly.
Rabban Gamliel holds that a kid's tail resembling a pig's tail is a blemish.
Rav Pappa: the pig-like tail refers to a curly tail even if thick, not only a thin one.
Restates the mishna clause on a kid's tail with fewer than three joints.
Rav Huna: a kid with two tail joints is a blemish, three is not; a lamb with three joints is a blemish, four is not.
Objects with a baraita that contradicts Rav Huna's joint counts, and concludes it refutes him.
Explains that Rav Huna was misled by the mishna's structure, which the baraita shows refers to a lamb in the second clause.
Rabbi Hananina ben Antigonus lists blemishes: a wart in the eye, damaged bones, a dislocated jaw, and uneven eyes or ears visible by sight.
Rabbi Yehuda's view on unequal testicles, which the Sages did not accept.
The Gemara asks whether a wart is, in fact, considered a blemish.
Raises a contradiction from a mishna listing animals on which firstborn slaughter is not done, including those with warts.
Objects that a wart is written in the Torah's list of blemishes, so it cannot be dismissed.
Reconciles by distinguishing a wart on the body from a wart on the eye.
The Gemara asks how the verse can distinguish body from eye, since it is stated without specification.
Offers an alternative: the cases differ by whether the wart has a bone.
Explains the distinction: a wart with bone is a blemish in the eye and not on the body, while a wart without bone is not a blemish on the body.
The Gemara asks whether an animal with a bone-less wart on its body is disqualified from sacrifice.
Cites a mishna in which Rabbi Eliezer says hanging flesh disqualifies a person but not an animal.
Concludes both mishnas concern the eye, with the black of the eye in one and the white in the other.
Objects that there are no blemishes in the white of the eye, so both cases must concern white.
Reish Lakish: a wart with hair in the white disqualifies an animal, while one without hair does not.
The mishna teaches that one large eye and one small eye is a blemish.
A baraita defines large as the size of a calf's eye and small as the size of a goose's eye.
The mishna teaches that uneven ears, visible by sight, are a blemish.
The Gemara asks how much smaller a second testicle may be according to the Rabbis.
A baraita states that according to the Aherim, even a second testicle no larger than a bean leaves the animal fit.
Mishna: a calf's tail that does not reach the leg joint is a blemish, since calves' tails extend beneath the joint as they grow.
The Gemara asks which leg joint the Sages meant.
Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus: the joint in the middle of the thigh.

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita identifies the leg joint as the upper one, where a camel's corresponding bone is visible but a calf's is not.
Mishna: for the blemishes listed, the firstborn is slaughtered outside the Temple and disqualified consecrated animals may be redeemed.
The Gemara asks why this additional clause is needed, since the first clause already taught the outside slaughter.
The first clause covers slaughter outside the Temple; the latter clause is needed to teach that consecrated animals with these blemishes may be redeemed.
The Gemara asks whether the redemption rule is obvious, since slaughter is already permitted for these blemishes.
Since Ila's three extra blemishes were rejected and other individual opinions follow, the mishna states an unattributed rule to show all of them are accepted.

Mishna: blemishes that do not permit slaughter outside the Temple, including inconstant tears, damaged gums, moist or dry boils, warts, old, sick or foul animals, and those with sins or killings proven by one witness or the owner.
Mishna: a tumtum or hermaphrodite may not be slaughtered in the Temple or in the rest of the country.
Rabbi Shimon says there is no greater blemish, so such an animal may be slaughtered.
The Rabbis say a hermaphrodite does not have firstborn status but is treated as non-sacred, to be shorn and used for labor.
Objects that garav and hazazit are blemishes in the Torah's list, so the mishna's exclusion of them is problematic.
A baraita identifies garav with hard earthenware-like boils and yalefet with the Egyptian hazazit.
Reish Lakish explains the name yalefet: it clings continuously to the invalid until death.
Resolves the contradictions: the Torah's hazazit is the Egyptian kind, while garav distinguishes moist boils, which heal, from dry ones, which do not.
Objects from a Deuteronomy verse that moist garav is included among boils from which one cannot be healed.
Offers three types of garav: dry inside and out, moist and curable, and the Egyptian kind dry inside but moist outside.
Cites Exodus on the boil breaking forth with avabuot upon man and animal to support the Egyptian garav.
The Gemara asks from where the rule about old, sick and foul-smelling animals is derived.
A baraita derives the exclusions from the word min in Leviticus, and the number of occurrences is considered.
Explains that each of the three exclusions is needed, since each case would otherwise be read differently.
Mishna: an animal with a transgression performed on it, or one that killed a person, is excluded.
The Gemara asks from where these rules are derived.
A baraita derives each exclusion from the word from in Leviticus, covering bestiality, worship, and goring.
Objects that these animals are liable to stoning, so why is a verse needed to exclude them.
The Gemara asks why a tumtum is not slaughtered in the Temple or outside, given the uncertainty about its sex.
Argues that the female organ of a hermaphrodite should count as a crack, a blemish permitting slaughter outside the Temple.
Abaye replies that the crack in the blemish list is comparable to a break, so it applies only where there is a bone.
Rava supports this by citing Leviticus on the leprosy appearance deeper than the skin, showing a crack in flesh is not a blemish.
Continues Rava's point: if a crack in flesh were a blemish, the Torah would need to write garav only for the repulsive case, which it does, so a crack in flesh is not a blemish.
Rabbi Yishmael says there is no greater blemish, so the hermaphrodite's female organ counts as a blemish.
Explains that Rabbi Yishmael does not agree with Abaye or Rava, since cracks and breaks are distinct blemishes, with a visible one counted as bad.

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava asks the reason for Rabbi Yishmael's ruling that a hermaphrodite is blemished: is it obvious to him, or is he uncertain whether it is a firstborn.
Rava asks what practical difference the two possible reasons make.
The difference concerns flogging for shearing or working with a firstborn, and whether a priest can claim the animal.
A baraita reports Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rabbi Yishmael that a hermaphrodite is a firstborn, which seems to show it is obvious to him.
Replies that Rabbi Yishmael may have spoken in the manner of if you say, so the matter is uncertain to him.
Another baraita derives from the word male in Leviticus that a tumtum and a hermaphrodite are excluded from burnt offerings.
The Gemara asks whose opinion this baraita reflects, since a verse excluding uncertainty would be odd.
If the baraita follows the later Rabbis, the exclusions come from one verse, which is difficult.
Rather, the baraita must follow Rabbi Yishmael, for whom the status of a hermaphrodite is obvious.
If Rabbi Yishmael is certain, the verse is needed only to exclude a hermaphrodite; if uncertain, a verse excluding uncertainty is strange.
The baraita follows the later Rabbis, and two verses exclude the female, tumtum and hermaphrodite respectively.
Rav Hisda: the dispute concerns only the hermaphrodite, while a tumtum is uncertain and so consecrated and not slaughtered.
Rava objects that if a tumtum is definitely male or female, valuation of a vow should follow that rule, which seems to conflict.

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why a baraita on the male valuation verse is said to include a male-certain animal but not a tumtum or hermaphrodite.
Omit the mention of a tumtum from the baraita, since it refers only to a hermaphrodite, a distinct entity.
Comes a baraita on women's valuation, which uses the male and female verses to exclude uncertain sexes.
Again, omit the tumtum from that baraita, which speaks only of a hermaphrodite.
A baraita on the peace offering, male or female, is cited as excluding a tumtum and hermaphrodite.
Omit the tumtum from this baraita as well.
A baraita on burnt offerings from cattle and sheep uses the repeated word male to exclude a tumtum and hermaphrodite.
Omit the tumtum from this baraita.
A baraita lists disqualified birds, including tumtum and hermaphrodite birds, as imparting impurity when pinched.
Rabbi Eliezer holds that a tumtum or hermaphrodite does not impart impurity, since the verses on male and female exclude them, not birds.
Omit the tumtum from the baraita, which conflicts with the first tanna's view.
Rabbi Elazar's baraita: a tumtum or hermaphrodite does not become consecrated or render another animal consecrated.
Shmuel explains that these animals cannot be consecrated by substitution.
Omit the tumtum from that baraita.
A variant baraita from Rabbi Elazar lists five animals that are not consecrated, including a tumtum and hermaphrodite.
If the tumtum is omitted, only four categories remain, which conflicts with the five-item list.
Remove the tumtum and insert an orphan animal, which is also disqualified as a sacrifice.
Proposes that the tumtum question is a dispute between tannaim.
Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rabbi Yishmael says a hermaphrodite is a firstborn with its blemish, while the Rabbis say it has no sanctity.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon derives from male that only a tumtum and hermaphrodite are excluded, showing a tumtum is a distinct entity.
If the tumtum is omitted here too, Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's view would equal the Rabbis', which seems wrong.
The real difference concerns a tumtum: the Rabbis treat a hermaphrodite as unsanctified but a tumtum as uncertain and so sacred.

42b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ben Yehuda says a tumtum is a distinct entity and not sacred at all.
Everyone agrees a tumtum is a distinct entity, so the doubt is only whether it is male or female.
Explains the dispute: if a tumtum urinates from the male place all agree it is male; for the female place, one view fears inversion and one does not.
Cites Rabbi Elazar's ruling about a firstborn animal urinating from the female place, which is non-sacred.
Rabbi Yohanan wonders who the Sage is who ignores the first tanna and Rabbi Yishmael, and whether he also ignores the later Rabbis per Rav Hisda.
Rabbi Yohanan does not hold Rav Hisda's view; he holds the later Rabbis, who treat a tumtum as a distinct entity, and Rabbi Elazar follows them.
Asks whose opinion Rabbi Elazar holds.
Reish Lakish: uncertainty about a tumtum applies only to a person, since a human's male and female organs share one place; for animals, urination location settles the sex.
Rav Oshaya objects that perhaps the male organ was inverted toward the female place, so the animal remains uncertain.
Abaye replies that the objection follows Rabbi Meir, who fears minority cases, and the halakha does not follow him.
Abaye bar Avin and Rav Hananya bar Avin: even per the Rabbis, a changed animal may be treated as changed, and the Sages disagree on that principle.
Proposes that the principle of an animal that changed in one respect is a dispute between tannaim.
A baraita: a tumtum's betrothal and levirate rules, with ruling that the tumtum performs halitza, while another baraita says the wife performs halitza and not levirate marriage.
The Sages assume all hold Rabbi Akiva's view that a naturally sterile eunuch neither performs halitza nor levirate marriage.
Asks whether the two baraitot really disagree on whether a changed tumtum is treated as changed.
The one who says the wife performs halitza and does not enter levirate marriage holds that a changed person is treated as changed.
Everyone agrees on the principle; the baraitot differ by tanna: Rabbi Eliezer permits levirate with a naturally sterile eunuch's wife, while Rabbi Akiva does not.
Asks which tanna holds Rabbi Akiva's view yet requires the tumtum's wife to perform halitza, since Rabbi Yehuda would treat it as a sterile eunuch.
A mishna: Rabbi Yehuda says a torn tumtum found to be male is like a naturally sterile eunuch and does not perform halitza.
The view is that of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, not his father.
A baraita: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says a tumtum does not perform halitza, since its covering could tear and it could be found a sterile eunuch.
Asks whether every torn tumtum is found male and never female, given the wording.
Rabbi Yosei frames the view as perhaps, so several uncertainties are considered, including that it could be found female.
An alternative reading: if found male it may also be a sterile eunuch, so it still cannot perform halitza.
Asks what the practical difference is between the two opinions, and Rava responds.

43a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the practical difference: for the widow, the tumtum's halitza is void according to Rabbi Yehuda but valid according to Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda.
Chapter-ending formula that names the chapter by its opening words.
Mishna: animal blemishes also disqualify a priest; additional priestly blemishes are listed, and Rabbi Yehuda permits a humped back while the Sages disqualify it, with a bald man disqualified.
Asks what a bald man, kere'ah, is.
A kere'ah lacks a row of hair from ear to ear; if he has such a row, he is fit for service.
The Gemara asks why the mishna says all animal blemishes disqualify a priest, since a wart is listed only for animals and cataract and tevallul only for people.
The blemishes are derived from one another by a verbal analogy, using the repeated scab and scurvy words in the verses for both people and animals.
Explains that the verbal analogy is valid only if the repeated words are superfluous, since otherwise a difference between people and animals could be raised.
Proves the repeated words are superfluous: a scab's disqualification would follow a fortiori from scurvy's, so the separate mention is needed for the analogy.
If animals and priests share the same blemishes, why not write all blemishes once and derive the rest by analogy?
If all were written for a person, animal-only blemishes such as closed hooves would be wrongly applied to animals.
If all were written for an animal, person-only blemishes such as a gibben or a sunken nose would wrongly be applied to people.
The Gemara asks why the Torah must list all common blemishes if each case could be written separately and the analogy used for the rest.
Rather, the school of Rabbi Yishmael holds that a repeated passage teaches a novel halakha, so the repetition serves the person-only and animal-only blemishes.
Rava asks why the Torah must write blemish disqualifications separately for priests, sacrificial animals and firstborns.
Each is necessary: a rule for priests alone could not be extended to animals, nor a firstborn rule to people, since each case has its own added stringency.
Sacrificial animals cannot be derived from firstborn animals, since a firstborn's sanctity is from the womb while other offerings are consecrated by a person.
Sacrificial animals cannot be derived from people or firstborns, since offerings have greater sanctity and many types.
Argues that if one case cannot be derived from one, perhaps it can be derived from two of the others.
The suggestion is rejected: the two cases differ in sanctity, so deriving from them would not work.
Rejects the other combinations too, since each pair differs in how sanctity arises or whether the subject is itself offered on the altar.
Mishna: beyond the animal blemishes, some blemishes apply to a priest even though they are not true defects.
Asks from where these priestly rules are derived.
Rabbi Yohanan derives it from Leviticus: a priest with a blemish may not offer, so he must be equal among Aaron's seed in appearance.

43b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what difference there is between a priest with a full blemish and one who is not equal among Aaron's seed.
A full-blemish priest who serves profanes the service, as Leviticus says he must not profane, while a non-equal priest does not.
Asks the difference between a priest not equal in lineage and one disqualified only by the appearance of a blemish.
The difference is the violation of the positive commandment: a non-equal priest transgresses it, while an appearance-only priest does not violate a Torah prohibition.
Explains the blemish terms: a pointed head, a turnip-like head, a hammer-like head, an indented head, a protruding back of head, and short or narrow necks.
Mishna on humped backs: Rabbi Yehuda deems them fit while the Rabbis disqualify them; the dispute concerns whether a bone is present.
Mishna: a kere'ah is disqualified from service.
Rava: a kere'ah is disqualified only if hair is missing at the back but present in front, and a person with hair at the back is fit.
Another version of the mishna's last clause, which Rava applies to a person with hair at the back only.
Rava's alternative: a person with hair in front and not at the back, or with no hair at all, is disqualified.
Rabbi Yohanan: bald priests, dwarves and priests with leaky eyes are disqualified because they are not equal among Aaron's seed.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yohanan needs to state this, since bald priests and dwarves are already listed in mishnayot.
He states it for leaky-eyed priests, which no mishna covers, and to show bald priests and dwarves are disqualified by Torah law, not rabbinic decree.
Objects that wherever the appearance of a blemish disqualifies, the tanna states so explicitly, so the same should apply to the rest of the list.
Rabbi Yohanan's statement is needed to rule out that extension to the whole list.
Persists: the tanna repeats the appearance-of-blemish reason wherever it applies, as with fallen teeth.
Rabbi Yohanan's point excludes a baraita holding that these priests are fit by Torah law and disqualified only by appearance.
Asks which tanna holds that such priests are fit by Torah law.
It is Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita derives from the word priests in Leviticus that Rabbi Yehuda includes bald priests in service.
Mishna: a priest with no eyebrows, or only one, is a gibben, the blemish named in the Torah.
Rabbi Dosa: a gibben is one whose eyebrows are so long they lie flat over his eyes.
Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus: a gibben is one with two backs and two spines.
The Gemara asks whether gibben itself means one without eyebrows.
Raises a contradiction from a baraita: gibben refers to many eyebrows, and the absence of eyebrows is derived from the word or.
Rava: the mishna is understood as deriving the disqualification of one lacking eyebrows from the exposition of or a gibben.
Restates Rabbi Dosa's view.
The Gemara asks whether a person with two backs and two spines can live, since the Sages discussed such a miscarriage as non-viable.
Rav Shimi bar Hiyya is told that Rabbi Hanina means a person with a crooked spine, who can survive but is disqualified.
Mishna: a harum is disqualified, defined by a sunken nose and several eye and sight defects; tearing and lost eyelashes are disqualifying.
A baraita derives from the word or in Leviticus that all nose blemishes, including retreating, blocked or drooping noses, disqualify.
Rabbi Yosei: a harum is only one who can paint both eyes as one.
The Sages reply that Rabbi Yosei has limited the definition of harum too far.

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rather, a priest with an abnormally sunken nose is a harum even if he does not paint both eyes as one.
The mishna's case: both of one's eyes are below.
The Gemara asks what the mishna means by both eyes above or both below.
If the phrases mean gazing upward or downward, the mixed case would be the same as the next case of seeing two stories as one.
Rather, the phrases refer to eyes set above or below their normal place, and the mishna adds a case of normal placement that still sees two floors as one.
Asks from where these rules are derived.
A baraita derives from the words in his eye that any eye blemish disqualifies, including a gaze upward, downward, or a seemingly mocked speaker.
A baraita: a blind priest is disqualified whether blind in both eyes or one, and the superfluous word ish includes pale spots and constant tears.
Rava asks why the Torah needs the words man, blind, cataract, tevallul and in his eye.
Each word is needed: blind alone would exclude only enucleated eyes, so man extends the rule to pale spots and tears.
Cataract covers impaired vision, and tevallul covers mixed black and white parts of the eye, each needed to avoid narrowing the rule.
Tevallul alone might suggest mixing, so in his eye is needed to cover eye deviations.
Summary: each eye word gives one category of eye blemish, from dimness through impairment, mixing, and deviation.
Mishna: those unable to look at the sun are disqualified.
Rav Yosef glosses this as those who hate the sun, and explains different eyes as one like ours and one like theirs.
Rav Huna pointed at Rav Yehuda, who had abnormal eyes, and Rav Yehuda took offense.
A baraita distinguishes the shekhavna, with eyebrows lying flat, from the zagdum, with one black and one white eyebrow, to challenge Rav Huna's reading.
The tanna calls any pair of limbs that are not identical zagdum, so the eyebrow case fits that term.
A baraita defines one whose eyes tear constantly: drooping or round eyes, with tears streaming or flowing.
A baraita defines zadir as strange eyes, lupin as too many eyelashes, and tamir as too few eyelashes.
The Gemara asks whether these count as full blemishes, since fallen eyelashes are only an appearance-based blemish in the mishna.
Not a contradiction: the mishna refers to eyelash roots remaining, while the baraita refers to roots that do not remain.
Mishna: calf-like or goose-like eyes, disproportionate body, limbs or nose, tzomem and tzome'a ears, a protruding lip, and teeth that fell out are disqualifying.
Rav: Moses was ten ammot tall.
Supports Rav with verses: Moses spread the tent over the Tabernacle, and the Tabernacle board is ten ammot long.
Rav Shimi bar Hiyya objects that this makes Moses disproportionate, which the mishna counts as a blemish.
Rav replies that the ten ammot refers to the cubit of a board, so Moses's limbs were proportionate.
A baraita: disproportion of the nose is measured by the size of the little finger.
The mishna's tzomem and tzome'a are blemishes, and a baraita adds the tzime'ah, which the Sages did not know until a long-eared goat was identified.
Rav Hisda: a hornless female goat and a horned female lamb are fit for the altar, since they are not true blemishes.
A baraita: certain seeming blemishes permit Temple slaughter but not outside; these include hornless goats and horned lambs, and the tzime'ah, tzomem and tzome'a.
Ameimar: removed horns with bone make the animal unfit but not redeemable; removed hooves with bone are unfit and redeemable.
A baraita says removed horns or hooves with bone are both unfit and redeemable, contradicting Rav Hisda.
Not a contradiction: the baraita refers to bone uprooted entirely, which is a full blemish, while the other refers to a horn merely hollowed.
Raises another contradiction from a baraita about a red cow with horns and hooves.

44b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: further disqualifying conditions, including sagging breasts, a swollen belly or navel, epilepsy, melancholy, and an overly long scrotum or penis.
Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba: Torah scholars may urinate in public but not drink water in public, since holding back harms the body.
A baraita repeats that rule and tells of a man who held back urine and was found to have a swollen belly.
Shmuel urinated on Shabbat when a sheet was spread for privacy, and his father offered him four hundred dinars to retract the lesson about privacy.
The father's reasoning: a man who cannot have a sheet spread should not endanger himself, so one should urinate even in public.
Mar bar Rav Ashi urinated while walking on bridge beams, and when told his mother-in-law was coming, said he would do it even in her ear.
A baraita: a man has two orifices, separated by a thin partition, and if they are punctured together he becomes barren.
Reish Lakish reads the verse on no barren male or female among you as meaning you must urinate as your cattle do, without holding back.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads the same verse as referring to barren students and unheard prayers, which come from humility like an animal.
Rav Pappa: one should urinate only on dust, not on earthenware or hard ground, since the water then returns to the Spring of Eitam.
Abaye: a woman should not stand openly before a child to urinate, but sideways is acceptable.
A baraita: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says holding back feces causes dropsy and holding back urine causes jaundice.
Rabba bar Rav Huna cites Rav Ketina and Reish Lakish: excess blood brings boils, excess semen leprosy, excess feces dropsy, and excess urine jaundice.
Mishna clause: one afflicted with a melancholy temper is disqualified.
The Gemara asks what the melancholy temper is.
A tanna says it means a fallen spirit, the spirit of a demon, has come upon him.
Mishna: one with an overly long scrotum or an overly long penis is disqualified.
A baraita defines meshuban as very large testicles and ba'al gever as an unnaturally long penis, and gives kayyan and garbeta as their synonyms.
The Gemara asks how long a penis must be to disqualify a priest.
Rav Yehuda points to the knee; a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov says reaching the knee disqualifies, and the opinions differ on going below it.
Mishna: a man with no testicles or only one is a mero'ah ashekh, a blemish stated in the Torah.
Rabbi Yishmael: mero'ah ashekh means one whose testicles were crushed.
Rabbi Akiva: mero'ah ashekh means one with wind in his testicles, meaning swollen.
Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus: the phrase refers to one whose appearance is especially dark.
Explains why each tanna reads the word differently, since each alternative would have required a different word, and that Rabbi Hanina rearranges letters homiletically.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Hanina's reading is identical to one with very black skin, which the mishna on 45b treats as disqualifying.
Rabbi Hanina's mishna teaches only that the mero'ah ashekh is disqualified, not the rule about black skin.
Mishna: next blemishes include legs that are crooked and bend inward, so the ankles or knees knock together.

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the mishna's list of leg and foot blemishes, starting with the bowlegged ba'al happikim.
Asks what an ikkel is.
An ikkel is one whose feet are placed together so the knees do not knock, i.e. bowlegged.
Mishna: a protuberance by the thumb or big toe, a protruding heel, and goose-like wide feet all disqualify a priest.
Mishna: fingers or toes fused together disqualify, unless fused only up to the middle joint; a cut extra digit with bone still disqualifies.
Mishna: an extra appendage on hands and feet is disputed by Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, and the ambidextrous case is disputed by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
A baraita derives from the verse on a broken foot that the or of or broken-footed includes all leg blemishes, such as knock-kneed and bowlegged.
A baraita on the ba'al hakippin and the shufnar, which Rabbi Yohanan defines by the size of leg protuberances.
Rabbi Elazar: a heel protruding means the lower leg emerges from the middle of the foot.
Mishna: wide, goose-like feet are a disqualifying blemish.
Rav Pappa: a flat foot counts as a blemish even if the toes are split, not only if the foot is wholly goose-like.
Mishna: fingers or toes lying one upon the other or fused are disqualifying.
A baraita: the broken-handed verse teaches that a broken hand disqualifies, and fused digits with cut or uncut connections are derived from it.
The Gemara interrupts: did you not say that a priest who separates his fingers is fit, so how is the uncut case derived?
The baraita answers that the case is uncut fusion above the middle joint, derived from the word or in the verse.
Mishna: an extra digit with bone is disqualifying even after it is cut, but if it lacks bone the priest is fit.
Rabba bar bar Hana, citing Rabbi Yohanan: this holds only if the extra digit can be counted along the back of the hand or foot.
A baraita: an extra digit with bone but no nail imparts impurity by contact and carrying and in a tent, and if counted with the others it adds to the 125 bones.
Rav Hisda cites Rav: an extra digit with bone and no nail imparts impurity by contact and carrying, not in a tent; Rabba bar bar Hana adds the counting condition.
Rabbi Yohanan: the Sages' ruling is like a prophetic statement, since either way it is difficult to explain.
Rav Huna bar Manoah cites Rav Aha son of Rav Ika: the Sages treated the digit as a barley-sized bone fragment, so it does not impart impurity in a tent.
Rav Pappa: the rule is a rabbinic decree that an uncounted digit imparts impurity by contact and carrying, based on the counted case.
Objects that if an uncounted digit is a limb in some sense, it should also impart impurity in a tent.
The Sages decreed this so people know the impurity is rabbinic, so they will not burn teruma or sacred items that are actually pure by Torah law.
Mishna in Oholot: a majority of bones or of the skeleton makes a corpse impure.
A baraita defines the majority of the skeleton as two calves and a thigh, and the majority of bones as 125.
Ravina asks Rava whether the tanna is teaching a number, since the count is obvious.
Rava: the tanna teaches that the count applies to a corpse with more or fewer bones, following the majority of people who have 248 bones.
Rabbi Yehuda cites Shmuel: students of Rabbi Yishmael boiled a prostitute's corpse and counted 252 limbs, and Shmuel explained the extra two hinges and two doors of a woman.
A baraita: Rabbi Elazar says a woman has hinges and Rabbi Yehoshua says doors, each supported by a verse.
Rabbi Akiva: a woman has a key, as the verse says He opened her womb.
Objects that the students of Rabbi Yishmael found no key, which challenges Rabbi Akiva's view.
Perhaps the small key dissolved when the corpse was boiled.
Rav: the limbs found only in a woman do not impart impurity in a tent, since the verse speaks of what is equal for all people.
Abaye objects that men also have hinges, citing Isaiah and Daniel's use of pains, which suggests the rule is not limited to women.
The Gemara replies that these are hinges of flesh, not counted limbs, and the same applies to men.
Argues that otherwise the 248 limbs could not be found in either a man or a woman, so the flesh-hinge answer must hold.

45b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna clause: an extra appendage on hands and feet, six on each, is the disputed case.
Rabbi Yitzhak: both sides derive their views from one verse about the Philistine champion with twenty-four fingers and toes, read as praise or as blemish.
Rabba asks why the verse needs to state twenty-four when six and six would already imply it.
All the details are needed: six and six alone could mean twelve, twenty-four alone could mean five and seven, and in number shows they are counted in one row.
A baraita tells of a man with twenty-four appendages whom Rabbi Tarfon blessed, supporting Rabbi Yehuda's view that they are not a blemish.
Mishna clause: a priest who controls both hands.
A baraita states a left-dominant priest is disqualified; the Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view that the weakness is in the right hand, while the Rabbis see strength in the left.

Mishna: the kushi, giḥor, lavkan, kipe'ah, dwarf, deaf-mute, imbecile, drunk, and those with marks are disqualified for service but fit for animal sacrifice; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar add remarks.
The Gemara glosses the colors: kushi is extremely black, giḥor extremely white, and lavkan extremely red.
Objects with an anecdote of a lukiyani lamb that turned out white, which contradicts that gloss.
Rather, a kushi is extremely black, a giḥor is extremely red, and a lavkan is extremely white, matching usage and the anecdote.
The kipe'ah is disqualified; Rav Zevid says it means one who is extremely tall.
Objects that the Holy One is praised for destroying the tall Amorites, so height cannot be a blemish.
Rav Pappa: the mishna refers to one who is long, emaciated and ugly, not one who is tall and well built.
Reish Lakish: tall, short, pale, or dark couples should not marry the same type, lest a child be extreme.
Mishna clause: the deaf-mute, imbecile and drunk are disqualified.
Objects that a drunk priest profanes the service, so drunkenness should have been listed with profaning blemishes, not with those not equal among Aaron's seed.
The mishna refers to intoxication by other agents, which does not profane the service; a baraita gives Rabbi Yehuda's view that drinking produces lashes and profanation.

Mishna: animals whose mother or offspring was slaughtered that day, tereifa, caesarean, bestiality, or killing are disqualified for sacrifice but not for priests; a priest with a forbidden wife or corpse impurity is disqualified until he vo
Mishna clause: the offspring case is fit for people.
The Gemara asks what human case the mishna's itself and its offspring rule could refer to.
If it refers to Aaron and his sons, a baraita limits the offspring prohibition to females, so a female priest would be needed, which is impossible.
The mishna refers to Aaron and his sons, with a male goat as the animal analogue, following Hananya, who applies the prohibition to both male and female.
Mishna clause: a priest who marries forbidden women is disqualified until he vows not to derive benefit from her.
A baraita: he vows, continues the rite, then descends and divorces her.
The Gemara asks how he can serve before divorcing, since a sage might dissolve the vow.
If the vow must be delineated, the sage would not dissolve it; but on the view that no delineation is needed, what can be said?
The vow is administered to the priest in public, so it cannot be dissolved.
The Gemara persists: on the view that a public vow cannot be annulled by a sage but another view allows annulment, what can be said?

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Completes the earlier point: the priest's share is given based on the consent of the public.
Ameimar's ruling: even on the view that a public vow can be annulled, a vow taken with public consent cannot be annulled for a discretionary matter, but can be for a matter of mitzva.
An example: Rav Aha bound a teacher by public-consent vow for hitting children, and Ravina annulled it because no one else was as meticulous.
Mishna clause: a priest who becomes impure through exposure to corpses is disqualified until he accepts a commitment.
The Gemara asks why a mere acceptance suffices here, while a vow is required for the priest who married forbidden women.
There the priest's desire overpowers him, so a vow is needed.
Chapter-ending formula that names the chapter by its opening words.
Mishna: the four categories of firstborn status for inheritance and for priestly redemption, and Rabbi Meir's view that a miscarriage opens the womb for inheritance only.
The Rabbis: a son is not exempt from priestly redemption unless the birth follows an animal-like miscarriage, with examples of women who were maidservants or gentiles.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: such a son is firstborn for both inheritance and priestly redemption, as the verse says whatever opens the womb among Israel.
Mishna: a son born to a man with children to a woman who had not given birth, or to one converted or freed while pregnant, is firstborn for redemption but not inheritance.

Mishna: births that are uncertain between mothers or between husbands, such as those with a priestly or Levite mother or a remarried widow, make the child firstborn for redemption but not inheritance.

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel: a head that emerged and went back does not exempt the next twin from firstborn redemption, but only in the case of a stillborn first fetus.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Shmuel's ruling.
Cites Genesis on whose nostrils had the breath of life: a viable fetus's head counts, while a non-viable one's does not.
Raises a difficulty from the mishna, which says a miscarriage's head exempts the next son, and asks what its head means.
Asks why the mishna did not say most of the fetus rather than its head.
The mishna needed the nine-month clause, and it used the same wording for uniformity; the first clause's head is meant to match.
The Gemara asks what the ruling adds if emerging head counts as birth.
Cites a mishna on animal fetuses, where a head that reaches out and returns still makes the fetus like a newborn.
The two rulings are needed separately because animals cannot teach humans, since a human's concealed opening makes the head's emergence less clear.
Cites a mishna that most of the head must emerge, and a forehead is that part, refuting Shmuel.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: a forehead exempts in all cases except inheritance, since recognition in inheritance requires the face; Deuteronomy 21:17 is cited.
Rabbi Yohanan: a forehead suffices even for inheritance.
Asks what the all-cases wording includes.
It includes a female convert whose child emerged forehead-first while she was a gentile, so no Jewish postpartum impurity or offering applies.
Objects to Rabbi Yohanan from a baraita: recognition requires the face with the nose, so the forehead alone is insufficient.
Adds a further proof from testimony about a dead husband, which requires the face with the forehead and nose, against Rabbi Yohanan.
Abaye, or Rav Kahana, cites Isaiah on recognition of the countenance as witnessing against them, meaning the face must be seen.
Testimony for remarriage is different, since the Sages were stringent about it, requiring more than for firstborn rules.
Asks whether the Sages were stringent there, since a mishna accepts hearsay and the testimony of women or slaves for remarriage.
The Sages were lenient about the end of the testimony, but not about identifying the dead person at the outset.
Introduces an alternative resolution, that Rabbi Yohanan can explain the difficulty another way.

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The requirement of he shall recognize for a firstborn's inheritance and the recognition of a husband's face are distinct matters.
Amoraim dispute a man who had children as a gentile and then converted: Rabbi Yohanan says he has no inheriting firstborn, Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says he does.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's position: the first son after conversion inherits a double portion.
Rabbi Yohanan's reason: the man already had the first of his strength before converting.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's reason: a convert is like a newborn, and each amora follows his line of reasoning.
The same dispute recurs: a man with children as a gentile who converted has already fulfilled the mitzva of being fruitful and multiplying.
Rabbi Yohanan says he has fulfilled the mitzva, while Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says he has not.
Rabbi Yohanan cites Isaiah: the world was not created in vain but formed to be inhabited.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: a convert is like a newborn, so as one who had no children he has not fulfilled the mitzva.
Both disputes must be stated, since each opinion could otherwise be read as limited to one case.
Likewise the reverse: Rabbi Yohanan's view on the mitzva does not show he holds the inheritance view, so both are needed.
Raises a difficulty from a mishna: a man who had no sons marries a woman who gave birth, and the child is a firstborn for inheritance but not for priestly redemption.
Asks from whom the woman had the child, and why the mishna specifies a convert or maidservant if the rule applies to any woman.
Suggests two cases in the mishna, one of which concerns a convert with earlier sons, which seems to contradict Rabbi Yohanan.
The mishna's child was born to a man without sons, and the reference to a gentile or maidservant serves only to exclude the redemption rule, excluding Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view.
Comes a baraita: a convert who had sons as a gentile and then fathered more has a firstborn for inheritance, which seems to prove against Rabbi Yohanan.
Ravina, or Rav Aha, says the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, whose view Rabbi Yohanan does not hold.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: a Levite's daughter's son is exempt from the five sela redemption payment, since her children from a gentile count as Levitical.
Asks whether this applies only to a priest or Levite father, and why the Levite daughter is singled out.
Objects with a verse from Numbers that lineage follows the father's house, not the mother's.
Rav Pappa: the case is a Levite's daughter by a gentile, where the mother's status governs, and even one who holds the child is disqualified still follows the mother.
Mar son of Rav Yosef, in Rava's name: the case is an Israelite father, and the verse about the opening of the womb makes the redemption depend on the mother's Levitical status.
Raises a difficulty against Rav Pappa from a mishna in which a woman's child by an Israelite may be a firstborn for redemption but not inheritance.
The mishna continues with cases of uncertain paternity between priest, Levite and Israelite mothers, giving redemption but not inheritance.
The inference from the mishna is that priests and Levites are exempt when the father is a gentile.
