Baraita on Numbers 35:10 and Yehuda ben Beteira: the Jordan itself is not part of the land of Canaan.
R. Shimon ben Yoḥai argues from Numbers 34:15 that the Jordan is part of the land of Canaan, as Jericho is.
R. Yoḥanan: the Jordan is called by that name only from Beit Jericho southward.
Asks for which halakha this matters, since a vow follows ordinary speech and the name applies everywhere.
It applies to animal tithe: the Jordan is a partition only south of Beit Jericho.
Baraita tracing the Jordan from the Cave of Pamyas through the lakes, named Jordan only below Beit Jericho.
R. Yoḥanan explains the name: the river descends from the city of Dan.
R. Abba tells Rav Ashi they learn the name from a verse rather than from a place tradition.
Judges 18:23 cites Dan naming Leshem after their father Dan, linking the river to the place name.
R. Yitzḥak identifies Leshem as Pamyas, and a baraita says the Jordan flows from the Cave of Pamyas.
Rav Kahana: the Jordan's source is the Cave of Pamyas, so a vow against its water covers the whole river.
Rav Kahana: blood originates in the liver, as R. Yitzḥak ruled about a decomposed liver's impurity.
Rav Kahana: all the world's water originates in the Euphrates, so a vow against it forbids all water.
Asks how a vow against Euphrates water can extend to all water, if one follows ordinary speech.
Rav Yehuda: the vow means water coming from the Euphrates, since all rivers draw from it.
Starts an objection, introduced by and isn't there, that continues beyond this daf.

55b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav: the high springs are ladders of the Euphrates, its waters seeping up through the ground.
Objects from Genesis 2:14 that the fourth river, the Euphrates, cannot be the source of the others.
Rav Naḥman or Rav Aḥa replies that the Euphrates was originally the fourth river, so Rav's view stands.
Baraita: R. Meir derives the Euphrates' name from Jeremiah 17:8, since its waters are many and fruitful.
Supports Shmuel's view that a river is purified by its banks' rising, as the baraita on the name shows.
Rav Ami reports Rav: rain in the West is a witness, and the rain counts for ritual purposes.
Shmuel's father made a mikveh for his daughters open on Nisan days and closed on Tishrei days.
Explains that Shmuel's father followed Rav's view, since drops may fall on creeping things and make the water pure.
Rain water was mostly used, and the mikveh was opened on Tishrei days.
Objects that Shmuel contradicts himself: he says water is purified by creeping things only from the Euphrates on Tishrei days.
Mishna: one who buys or receives an animal as a gift is exempt from animal tithe.
Asks from where this rule about purchase and gift is derived.
Rav Kahana cites Exodus 22:28-29 on the firstborn of your herd and flock, which shows the obligation applies only to the owner.

56a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Derives from the firstborn son that purchased or gifted animals are exempt from animal tithe.
Objects that the verse linking animals to the firstborn is written about firstborn redemption, not animal tithe.
Since firstborn animals are sanctified at birth, the verse's so you shall do applies to animal tithe.
Rejects applying the verse to sin and guilt offerings, since animal tithe, like a son, is not brought for sin.
Rejects applying the verse to burnt and peace offerings, since animal tithe cannot be brought as a vow or gift.
Rejects applying the verse to the appearance offering, since animal tithe has no fixed time, unlike the three festivals.
If animal tithe is derived from the firstborn, why does R. Asi report R. Yoḥanan that purchased fetuses are tithed?
Rava: the verse excludes purchased animals only from the time they are fit for the altar, not in the womb.
R. Asi reports R. Yoḥanan: ten fetuses bought in the womb, born after purchase, all enter the tithe pen.
Objects from the mishna that one who buys or receives an animal as a gift is exempt from animal tithe.
R. Elazar says R. Yoḥanan appeared to him in a dream, and the verse excludes purchased animals only at the time of doing.
R. Shimon b. Elyakim objects with a baraita: a purchased animal before its time is exempt, so a fetus should be too.
R. Elazar replies the baraita is not reliable, or follows R. Shimon b. Yehuda, since a firstborn is sanctified before its time.
A tanna taught before Rav that an animal given to a prostitute and bought back enters the tithe pen.
The tanna objects that such an animal is disqualified as purchased, so the teaching seems wrong.
That tanna missed R. Yoḥanan's ruling, so the baraita applies to a fetus bought back from the prostitute.

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the animal must be bought back if the prostitute could tithe it herself, since it was in the womb.
Objects: the baraita could concern a Jewish prostitute who tithes the animal herself.
Explains that the baraita teaches a Jewish prostitute's payment does not count as payment to a prostitute.
Abaye's view: payment from a gentile prostitute is forbidden for sacrifice, while a Jewish one's is permitted.
Abaye derives the gentile-prostitute rule by verbal analogy from the word abomination in Deuteronomy 23:19 and Leviticus.
Abaye explains a priest with a gentile prostitute is not flogged, since her children are not his seed.
Mishna: brothers who share an inheritance and pay the premium are exempt from animal tithe, and vice versa.
Baraita on Exodus 13:12: animal tithe applies only to an animal owned by one owner, not to partners.
Asks why this verse is applied to animal tithe when it is written about firstborn animals.
Since firstborn sanctity applies to partnerships, the verse is used for animal tithe, excluding partnership animals.
R. Yirmeya: depending on how the estate was divided, brothers may owe the premium, animal tithe, both, or neither.
Elaborates R. Yirmeya's cases: divided money versus animals determines whether the estate is treated as individually owned.
Asks why it is needed to state the case where animals were divided but money was not.
Without the teaching, one might think division of animals shows intent to divide all, so the premium would be owed.
R. Anan: if kids and goats are divided by swapping whole species, the brothers are treated as strangers.
R. Naḥman: even a division of kids for kids and goats for goats is not treated as a share from the outset.
R. Elazar: the same distinction applies to nine large goats for ten kids, by the trade-value of each.
R. Yoḥanan: even nine goats for nine goats and ten kids for ten kids are not treated as a share from the outset.

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yoḥanan is consistent with his own line of reasoning, as R. Asi reports his view on inherited property.
R. Yoḥanan: brothers who divided inherited land are treated as buyers from each other and return it in the Jubilee.
Explains why both halakhot are needed: animal tithe could otherwise be limited, or land treated as a sale only.
Explains that the field ruling might be read as stringency or as restoring the original state, so both cases are taught.
Baraita objects to retroactive designation: the ten lambs given for a dog should not all be forbidden if one could be set aside.
Rav Ashi reconciles: when values differ, the extra value of the dog is spread over all ten lambs, so all are forbidden.
Mishna: all animals enter the tithe pen except crossbreeds, tereifot, caesarean births, animals under eight days and orphans.
Asks from where these exclusions are derived.
Baraita on Leviticus 22:27 derives each exclusion from its phrase: diverse kinds, caesarean, under eight days, orphan.
R. Yishmael b. R. Yoḥanan b. Beroka applies the verbal analogy of under to extend these exclusions to animal tithe.
Asks what the mishna's word all is meant to include.
The word all includes animals with sexual defects, idol-linked or bestial animals, and tumtum and hermaphrodites, per the baraita.
Objects that if the mishna's tanna derives from sacrificial animals, these disqualified categories should also be excluded.
The Torah itself includes these categories: Leviticus 22:25 treats corruption as a blemish.
Teaching of the school of R. Yishmael: corruption always means licentiousness or idol worship.
Cites Genesis 6:12 and Deuteronomy 4:16 as the two senses of corruption: licentiousness and idolatry.
Corruption disqualifies only when a blemish does, so licentiousness or idolatry disqualifies only where a blemish does.
Applies this to animal tithe: since a blemish does not disqualify tithe (Leviticus 27:33), neither does licentiousness or idolatry.
Classifies each category: bestiality and sexual acts are licentiousness; idol-linked animals are idolatry; prostitute payment is licentiousness.
The first tanna holds a tumtum is an uncertain case, so tumtum animals are tithed.
R. Shimon b. Yehuda: uncertain cases are excluded from sacrifices, so tumtum and hermaphrodite animals are not tithed.
Baraita: all animals are tithed except crossbreeds and tereifot, per R. Elazar b. R. Yehuda; R. Akiva adds caesarean, young and orphan.
Asks what the first tanna holds, given that his exclusions would also follow from sacrificial animals.
He derives the exclusion by verbal analogy, and the caesarean and orphan cases are learned from the same analogy.

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The tanna follows R. Shimon, who counts a caesarean animal as a proper birth, and not R. Yoḥanan.
The not-yet-arrived animal is tithed, following R. Shimon b. Yehuda's view that such animals are tithed.
An orphan whose mother's hide remains is not an orphan, following R. Yehoshua's consistent view on slaughtered mothers.
R. Yishmael b. Satriel testifies that locally they clothe a newborn in its dead mother's hide, explaining the mishna's rule.
R. Yishmael b. Satriel reports further local wonders: huge lettuce leaves and a cedar that sixteen wagons passed over.
R. Yishmael b. Satriel reports an egg of the bar yokhani bird that drowned sixty cities and broke three hundred cedars.
Objects that the bird leaves its eggs on the ground, according to Job 39:13-14, so the egg could not have fallen like that.
Rav Ashi explains the egg was unfertilized, so the bird threw it down since it would never hatch.
Mishna: three times a year, before Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, are gathering times for animal tithe, per R. Akiva.
Ben Azzai gives the dates as twenty-ninth of Adar, first of Sivan and twenty-ninth of Av.
R. Elazar and R. Shimon give the dates as first of Nisan, first of Sivan and twenty-ninth of Elul.
They chose twenty-ninth of Elul rather than first of Tishrei, because tithing is not done on a festival.
R. Meir says the new tithe year begins on first of Elul, while ben Azzai tithes Elul-born animals separately.
Mishna: under R. Elazar and R. Shimon, animals born from first Tishrei to twenty-ninth Elul are tithed together.
The three gathering times matter because animals may be sold and slaughtered before gathering, but not after.
Asks why there are specifically three gathering times in the year.
Rabba bar Sheila: three times collect winter-born, spring-born and summer-born animals.
Asks what distinguishes these three particular times, before Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot.
R. Tanḥum son of R. Ḥiyya of Akko begins his explanation of the three times.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Animals must be available for pilgrims, and an owner prefers to perform the mitzva with his money before selling.
Asks why the gathering time is called a threshing floor.
R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda explains that adjacent means not less than fifteen days.
Asks what the word peras is inferred from.
R. Abbahu: peras means half the time for studying Passover laws, which per a baraita is thirty days, or two weeks per Rabban Shimon.
Ben Azzai gives the dates as twenty-ninth of Adar and first of Sivan.
Asks what principle underlies the dispute between R. Akiva and ben Azzai.
R. Akiva treats Adar as sometimes twenty-nine or thirty days, so he gives no fixed date; ben Azzai fixes one for practical reasons.
Ben Azzai gives the last gathering time as the twenty-ninth of Av.
Ben Azzai's consistent view: Elul-born animals are tithed separately, so the gathering must precede Elul.
R. Elazar and R. Shimon give the dates as first of Nisan and first of Sivan, as the Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel view explains.
R. Elazar and R. Shimon's third date, twenty-ninth of Elul, follows from their view that Tishrei begins the new tithe year.
Restates the mishna: twenty-ninth of Elul is used because tithing is not done on the festival of Rosh HaShana.
Objects that the Gemara should derive the rule from the need to distinguish new and old animals alone.
The mishna gives two reasons: distinguishing new from old animals, and the festival prohibition on applying the marking paint.
R. Meir says the tithe year begins on first of Elul, while ben Azzai treats Elul-born animals separately.
Ben Azzai: since these Sages and those disagree, Elul-born animals are tithed by themselves.
Asks why ben Azzai does not simply decide whose reasoning is more plausible.
Objects that ben Azzai dismissed all Sages except Rabbi Akiva, so he could not have been unable to judge.
R. Yoḥanan: the Sages' views came by tradition from the prophets, so logic cannot settle the dispute.
Baraita: ben Azzai's exact rule on which animals born in Av, Elul and Tishrei combine for tithing.
Asks why this needs stating, since the obvious view is that set times separate animals.
The baraita is needed lest one think the gathering times separate animals too, which they do not.
Cites the mishna: five born before and five after Rosh HaShana do not combine, but before and after the gathering do.
Rava: by ben Azzai's view, animals born in Av, Elul and Tishrei are gathered together into the pen to be tithed.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava: one takes one of the Elul-born animals and the rest are exempt, whichever date is the new year.
Challenges Rava: why are the Tishrei-born animals exempt, given the verse demands a definite tenth.
Asks whether it is obvious that the tithe is taken from the Elul-born animals.
Rava states it so that one does not think the Sages would forbid taking the tithe from Elul animals.
Mishna: how tithing is done, counting through a narrow opening with red paint, and which tithes stand after an error.
Baraita: the pen has a narrow opening so the mothers outside call the young animals out to pass one at a time.
Asks why the animals should not simply be pushed out, or lured out with vegetables.
Rav Huna: the mothers' role is a rabbinic decree because of the purchased animal and the orphan.
Baraita on Leviticus 27:32: the animal must pass under the rod, counted one by one, and the tenth is sanctified.
Baraita on Leviticus 27:9: the tenth is sanctified even if not called tenth, and one pulled out uncounted is not tithe.
R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda says that the one removed uncounted from ten is tithe.
Asks what R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda's reason is.
Abba Elazar ben Gomel: Numbers 18:27 equates teruma and tithe, so tithe is taken by estimate and thought, as teruma is.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abba Elazar: grain tithe and animal tithe are both taken by estimate and thought, since the verse links them.
Rava: a tenth animal that remains in the pen is sacred on its own, even without leaving it.
Asks from where Rava derives this, since the baraita on the tenth animal seems to show otherwise.
Cites the baraita: the verse says the tenth shall be sacred in any case, even if not called tenth.
Objects that the baraita may mean the tenth is sacred only if it is called tenth, or simply that it is not.
Baraita: the owner calls the ninth animal tenth, and the real tenth leaves the pen unnamed and is sacred.
Objects that in that case the tenth was singled out as it left, unlike one that stayed in the pen.
Baraita: if the tenth dies in the pen, the others are exempt from tithe, since the tenth was set aside.
Asks why the others are exempt, if not because the tenth is sacred even without leaving the pen.
Objects that the others may be exempt because they were counted in a tally fit to reach ten.
Rava's principle: a tally fit to reach ten exempts from tithe.
Baraita: if the tenth remains in the pen, the ninth is non-sacred and the tenth is tithe, so Rava's view is supported.
Objects: but a baraita teaches that the ninth animal in that case is non-sacred, which conflicts with Rava.
A tanna taught before Rav Sheshet a ruling about the ninth and tenth animals.
Rav Sheshet asks whose view this is; the answer is R. Shimon b. Yehuda, quoting R. Shimon.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ninth animal is not sanctified unless the tenth designation is removed from the tenth animal.
A kal vachomer from the eleventh animal, which is sanctified only under that condition, is offered.
The objection: the eleventh and ninth cases differ, so the kal vachomer does not hold.
An alternative distinction: the eleventh is sanctified only after the tenth leaves the pen, so the kal vachomer fails.
Reply: the ninth is sanctified before the tenth leaves the pen, so the distinction stands and the rival view is rejected.
Rava states that a tally fit to reach ten exempts the animals counted in it.
Asks where Rava gets this principle from.
Proposes a source in the mishna's exemption ruling, reading it as based on a tally fit to reach ten.
Objects that the mishna's exemption may come from the tenth animal having been tithed instead.
Rejects that reading: the latter clause refers to animals already tithed, so the exemption comes from the tally.
Objects again that tithed refers only to the tenth animal, so the mishna proves nothing for Rava.
Rava brings a verse from Leviticus 27:32 that only animals passing under the rod are tithed.
Asks what the verse means by animals that already passed under the rod.
Explains that the phrase excludes animals already tithed, so it must mean animals exempted by a tally, which proves Rava.
A baraita is introduced as agreeing with Rava.
The baraita about ten lambs with deaths before and after counting supports Rava's principle.
Rava's fourteen-lamb case: if the last four leave through the six's opening, one is tithed; otherwise the groups are exempt or combined.
Rava's second fourteen-lamb case, with the groups of four and six reversed, and the same tithing outcomes.
Rava's third fourteen-lamb case, with four and four leaving first and six remaining, and the outcomes that follow.
Asks what Rava is teaching here, since he already said the tally principle once.
Answers that the repeat is needed for a tally that is only uncertain to reach ten, which still exempts.
Rava states that with fifteen lambs one may not pre-select ten and tithe one, since that would leave the rest exempt.
Rava gives the correct procedure: bring all fifteen in, remove ten, tithe one, and the rest combine with later animals.
A baraita teaches the same ruling for fifteen lambs, supporting Rava.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava's rule continues: one may not pre-select ten, but must bring all in, remove ten, tithe the tenth, and the rest combine later.
The Gemara objects that a baraita about nineteen lambs contradicts Rava, since it exempts the rest with no combining.
Rav Huna bar Sehora explains the baraita with a pen of two openings, so every lamb left within a tally fit to reach ten.
Objects that the baraita could instead be about miscounting, where the tenth lamb is designated first, so the rest are exempt.
Objects that the baraita could be about pair-by-pair counting with one opening, which still conflicts with the ruling about nine remaining.
Rabbi Naḥman bar Yitzhak praises Rav Huna bar Sehora's mother for raising a son who taught Rava's halakha correctly.
Mishna: if two animals emerged as one and were counted as two, the ninth and tenth are flawed through miscounting.
Mishna continues: if counted with errors, all three are sacred with different statuses, and Rabbi Meir holds the eleventh makes a substitute.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that a substitute cannot create another substitute, so Rabbi Meir's view is impossible.
The Sages defend Rabbi Meir: if the eleventh were a substitute it would not be sacrificed, so it is not sanctified.
The general principle: if the name of the tenth was not removed from the tenth animal, the eleventh is not sanctified.
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that a tenth counted pair by pair, or hundred by hundred, is sanctified according to his count.
Asks what Rabbi Yoḥanan means by sanctified according to his count.
Rav Mari explains it is sanctified according to the designation the owner gave, such as the tenth pair.
Rav Kahana explains it is sanctified according to the animal's position in the group, regardless of the designation.
Cites the mishna about double counting as support for Rav Mari's position that designations matter.
Objects that according to Rav Kahana the mishna's flaws cannot be explained, since the ninth and tenth would be counted correctly.
Explains that Rabbi Yoḥanan meant only a deliberate pair-by-pair count, while an animal that left by itself keeps its order.
Brings a baraita about counting backward, where the tenth in order is sanctified, as support.
Objects that under Rav Mari the tenth animal here was designated as number one, so it should not be sanctified.
Rava answers that Persian counting uses units of ten and calls each unit one, so no contradiction arises for Rav Mari.

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna's case restated: the ninth called tenth, the tenth called ninth, and the eleventh called tenth, all three sanctified.
A baraita introduces the question of where the sanctity of all three is derived.
Derives it from Leviticus 27:32: the tenth that passes under the rod is sacred, and mistaken designations are included.
Argues by analogy: as the true tenth is sanctified only when adjacent to ten, a mistaken designation is too.
Objects that a baraita says the mistaken designation is unique, so both the ninth and eleventh cannot be sanctified.
Answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, who requires silence when the ninth leaves the pen.
Explains Rabbi Elazar's position: he follows Rabbi Yehuda on substitution and his father on not substituting twice.
Rava's case: two animals leave together as ninth, both called ninth, so the tithe and non-sacred animal intermingle.
Rava's case: two animals leave together as ninth, both called tenth, so the tithe and the ninth intermingle.
Rava's cases: two animals leave together as tenth and both called tenth or both called eleventh, with the outcomes listed.
Asks why the case of two animals leaving together as tenth is needed, since it seems identical to the ninth case.
Answers that this clause teaches that two animals leaving together are both sanctified even without removing the tenth's name.
Rav Kahana sits and recites this halakha to his students.
Rav Ashi objects that the name of the tenth was not removed, so the mishna's principle should exclude this case.
Cites the mishna's principle that the eleventh is not sanctified unless the tenth's name was removed, as support for Rav Ashi.
Rav Kahana replies that the principle applies only when animals leave one after another, not when two leave together.
Objects that the mishna explicitly covers the tenth and eleventh both called tenth, so what does the principle add.
Rav Kahana answers that the principle includes a tenth that the owner did not speak about, and was not removed from it.
Objects that a baraita about two animals leaving together as tenth conflicts with this explanation of the mishna.
Rav Ashi rebuts: the baraita concerns one animal whose head came out early, so the name was removed and both are sanctified.
Objects that the baraita says neither came out before the other, which contradicts Rav Ashi's reading.
Explains that not coming out before means the animal did not fully emerge but returned and mixed with the others.
Asks whose opinion the baraita follows, since Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would hold calling the tenth eleventh does not remove its status.
Answers that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view applies only when the owner has many animals, where the word eleventh means one set of ten.
Asks which statement of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is meant, given a baraita is cited.
The baraita records Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's principle on removing the tenth's name.
Rava explains the case is one where the owner has many animals, so calling it eleventh means one set of ten.
Baraitot give conflicting rulings for two animals leaving together as tenth: graze until blemished, sacrifice, or both die.
Resolves the conflict: the grazing ruling follows the Rabbis, who forbid bringing offerings where their eating time could be cut short.

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The tanna's ruling that both animals are sacrificed follows R. Shimon, who allows bringing offerings into a disqualifying situation.
The ruling that both must die follows R. Yehuda, who holds that a substitute for animal tithe must be left to die.
The Gemara objects from a mishna: by inference, R. Yehuda holds the eleventh animal is sacrificed rather than put to death.
Proposed reply, later rejected: R. Meir spoke according to his own view, so nothing follows about R. Yehuda's opinion.
A baraita shows R. Yehuda's view that the eleventh animal is sanctified to be sacrificed, so it is not left to die.
A Sifra verse on peace offerings from the herd includes the eleventh animal mistakenly designated as animal tithe.
The Sifra excludes the ninth animal by reasoning that consecration sanctifies a substitute only after the original is sanctified.
The unattributed Sifra is identified as R. Yehuda's teaching, showing he holds the eleventh is sacrificed as a peace offering.
Reply: R. Shimon b. Abba explains the baraita concerns present-day tithe, where animals die out of fear of mishap.
Why does the baraita specify two animals, since the same ruling would seem to apply even to a single animal?
Reply: the tanna uses the it-is-unnecessary style; one animal needs no teaching, but two, with greater loss, must die.
Rav Pappi, in Rava's name, rules that a mistaken ninth-as-tenth by an agent is sanctified, but the eleventh is not.
Rav Pappa disagrees: even a ninth-as-tenth designation by an agent is not sanctified, since an agent acts only for the owner's benefit.
Asks how this case differs from a mishna on an agent separating teruma, where the owner's intention governs.
The teruma mishna: an agent follows the owner's intention, and a separation miscalculated by ten still counts as teruma.
The Sages answer that teruma differs because people vary in generosity, so the agent's estimate is valid; animal tithe is a mistake.
Closing colophon marking the end of the chapter and of the tractate Bekhorot.
